The Residue of Proof

Suﬀiciency, History, and Repair in Automated Reasoning



                       Flyxion

                Independent Researcher


                   October 2026

Preface




Automated reasoning systems have become dependable producers of verified statements:
a satisfiability solver emits a refutation that a small checker accepts, a proof assistant elab-
orates a script into a term that a kernel typechecks, a rewrite engine normalizes an expres-
sion and a certificate says the normalization was sound. In each case the output of the
process is a verdict together with evidence that a trusted component can examine. This
book is about what such an output is not, and about what it would have to retain in order
to remain useful to a scientist who relies on it.

  A verified result can be correct and still fail its user in at least three ways.  It may be
correct about a formal object that is not the object of interest, so that the bridge from the
formal statement to the observation carries obligations no kernel can discharge.  It may
be correct and fragile, valid for the constants it was checked against and silent about the
neighbouring ones. And it may be correct and opaque: the history of the search that found
it, the options that were refused, the alternatives that were tried, may be the only thing
that would let a later reader repair it when an assumption changes, and that history is
precisely what compression throws away. The central claim is that these three failures
have a common mathematical form. In each, a function that was needed was not constant
on the fibres of the representation that was kept.



Structure.  Part I sets out proof systems and search as transition systems and develops the
classical machinery used throughout: inference systems and fairness, resolution and unifi-
cation, rewriting and normal forms. Part II treats the decision procedures and kernels that
supply certificates in practice: conflict-driven clause learning and its proof formats, the-
ory combination, the kernel architecture of proof assistants, and the trusted base. Part III
is the core. It defines verification obligations, suﬀiciency of a representation relative to a
declared task family, stability regions and repair, and inheritance along transformations.
Part IV applies the same structure to the steps of a search, asking when a search may dis-
card possibilities while keeping the guarantees that justify it.  Part V turns to scientific
use: correspondence with observations, mutation of verified artifacts as an experiment on
the claims of Part III, and a negative result treated as a method. Part VI collects the three
principles and an honest account of what has been proved.



Standards of proof.  Results internal to the argument are proved. Classical external theo-
rems are stated precisely and cited; they are listed in Appendix A. Several statements were
also checked by computation, as recorded in Chapter 20, and these checks are marked as
checks and not as proofs. No theorem of the book has been mechanized in a proof assistant.
Where the book describes experimental work reported elsewhere, the chapters prove what

such reports can and cannot support and do not reproduce the data.


A note on vocabulary.  The verbs pop, refuse, bind and collapse are used in Part IV for the
operations on a search world, following earlier manuscripts of the author on binding and
on disposition calculi [35, 36]. Every definition needed is restated, and nothing from those
manuscripts is assumed.


Reading. A reader interested only in the classical material can read Parts I and II alone;
they are independent of the rest. A reader interested in the argument can begin with Chap-
ter 1, Chapter 10, and Chapter 20. Each chapter closes with a boxed statement of what it
establishes and with exercises, some of which are open-ended extensions flagged as such.

Chapter 1

Proof Systems as Transition Systems




Automated reasoning is usually described by what it produces: a verdict that a statement
holds, together with some evidence for the verdict. This chapter fixes the minimal vocab-
ulary needed to say precisely what the evidence is, what checks it, and what the process
that found it leaves behind. Everything later in the book is a refinement of three objects
introduced here: a checker, a producer, and the residue that remains when the producer’s
work is compressed into a checked derivation.


1.1  Proof systems and checkers

Definition 1.1 (Proof system). A proof system is a quadruple S = (Φ, D, Chk, Val) where
  (i) Φ is a set of statements, each a finite string over a fixed finite alphabet;
 (ii) D is a set of derivations, each a finite string over a fixed finite alphabet;
 (iii) Chk ⊆D × Φ is a decidable relation, the checking relation; and
 (iv) Val ⊆Φ is a set of valid statements, defined semantically and not required to be
     decidable or even recursively enumerable.
The system is sound if Chk(d, φ) implies φ ∈Val, and complete if φ ∈Val implies Chk(d, φ)
for some d ∈D. The set of theorems is Th(S) = {φ ∈Φ : ∃d ∈D. Chk(d, φ)}.

   Decidability of Chk is the single structural requirement, and it is the reason a proof sys-
tem is useful at all: whoever holds a candidate derivation can settle its status by a termi-
nating computation, regardless of how the candidate was obtained. Validity, by contrast,
is a semantic notion. The central role of the gap between Th(S) and Val is already visible:
soundness says the former is inside the latter, completeness says they coincide.

Proposition 1.2 (Theorems are enumerable).  If D is effectively enumerable then Th(S) is re-
cursively enumerable. If in addition S is sound and complete, Val is recursively enumerable.

Proof. Enumerate the pairs (d, φ) ∈D × Φ in a fixed dovetailed order, run the decision
procedure for Chk on each pair, and output φ whenever the check succeeds. This lists
exactly Th(S). If S is sound and complete then Th(S) = Val.                ■

   Proposition 1.2 is the formal reason that every complete proof system for first-order
validity yields a semi-decision procedure and no more; Chapter 2 returns to this with
Church’s theorem.

                                       2

1.2. PRODUCERS AND THE INDEPENDENCE OF SOUNDNESS                    3


Example 1.3 (An implicational Hilbert system). Let Φ be the set of formulas built from
propositional variables with the connective →. Let a derivation be a finite sequence of
formulas, each of which is an instance of one of the schemes

      K : A →(B →A),    S : (A →(B →C)) →((A →B) →(A →C)),

or follows from two earlier lines A and A →B by modus ponens. Define Chk(d, φ) to hold
when d is such a sequence ending in φ. The relation is plainly decidable. With Val the set
of formulas true under every Boolean valuation, soundness holds: instances of K and S are
tautologies, and modus ponens preserves truth under a fixed valuation, so an induction
on the length of d shows that every line is a tautology.
  A derivation of p →p:

              1.  (p →((p →p) →p)) →((p →(p →p)) →(p →p))  S
              2.  p →((p →p) →p)                      K
              3.  (p →(p →p)) →(p →p)                MP 2, 1
              4.  p →(p →p)                          K
              5.  p →p                           MP 4, 3

The five-line certificate is longer than the truth table for p →p, which has two rows. This is
the first instance of a pattern that recurs throughout the book: a derivation is not a compact
summary of why a statement holds, but a record in a fixed idiom of one way to establish
it.


1.2  Producers and the independence of soundness

Definition 1.4 (Producer). A producer for S is any partial function P  : Φ ⇀D. No assump-
tion of computability, correctness, or termination is made. The set of statements accepted
from P is
              Acc(P) = {φ ∈Φ : P(φ) is defined and Chk(P(φ), φ)}.

Theorem 1.5 (Independence of soundness). Let S be sound. For every producer P, Acc(P) ⊆
Val. Conversely, if S is complete then there is a producer P ∗with Acc(P ∗) = Val.

Proof. If φ ∈Acc(P) then Chk(P(φ), φ), hence φ ∈Val by soundness. For the converse, by
completeness choose for each φ ∈Val a derivation P ∗(φ) with Chk(P ∗(φ), φ), and leave
P ∗undefined elsewhere.                                    ■


  The theorem is elementary, but its consequences are the organizing principle of the
whole subject.  The assurance attached to an accepted statement depends only on the
checker; the producer may be heuristic, learned, probabilistic, buggy, or adversarial
without affecting it. The cost is paid in a different currency. A producer’s failure to deliver
a derivation carries no information about validity.

  Discipline of non-certification. Let φ /∈Acc(P). Nothing follows about φ ∈Val
  unless a separate argument shows that P is complete on φ. Failure of certification is
  not certification of failure.

4                  CHAPTER 1. PROOF SYSTEMS AS TRANSITION SYSTEMS

1.3  Statements as translations

The statement φ ∈Φ that a checker reads is rarely the claim a person intends. A physicist
or mathematician states a claim ψ in a vocabulary of their own, and a translation τ renders
it into the checker’s language.

Definition 1.6 (Adequate translation). Let (Ψ, True) be a set of intended claims with a
truth predicate True ⊆Ψ. A map τ  : Ψ →Φ is adequate for S if τ(ψ) ∈Val implies
ψ ∈True.

Proposition 1.7 (Composition of assurance). If S is sound and τ is adequate, then Chk(d, τ(ψ))
implies ψ ∈True.

Proof. Soundness gives τ(ψ) ∈Val, adequacy gives ψ ∈True.               ■

  The proposition has a precise and uncomfortable reading. The checker, however small
and trusted, certifies only τ(ψ) ∈Val. Whether this carries over to ψ is a property of τ
and of the notion True, neither of which the checker examines. In the vocabulary of later
chapters, τ is a bridge hypothesis, and a verified result is the pair of a checked derivation and
an unchecked bridge. Chapter 9 organizes these obligations; for the moment the point is
that adequacy of τ is not a theorem of S, and in general cannot be, since True may refer to
a world outside the system.


1.4  Search as a transition system


Producers in practice are searches. A producer begins from a goal, repeatedly applies rules
that extend or restrict a partial structure, and stops when a derivation can be read off.

Definition 1.8 (Search procedure). A search procedure for S is a tuple R = (Σ, →, ι, F, ext)
where Σ is a set of states, →⊆Σ × Σ a transition relation, ι : Φ →Σ an initialization map,
F ⊆Σ the final states, and ext  : F →D an extraction map. A run on φ is a finite path
ι(φ) = s0 →s1 →· · · →sn with sn ∈F; its trace is the sequence (s0, . . . , sn) and its output
is ext(sn).

   Define the producer PR by choosing, for each φ that admits a run, the output of some
run (the choice is immaterial for what follows). Then PR falls under Theorem 1.5. We
separate two properties of a procedure.

Definition 1.9 (Internal soundness, trace-faithfulness). R is internally sound if for every run
on φ ending in sn we have Chk(ext(sn), φ). It is trace-faithful if the trace can be recovered
from the output together with φ, that is, if the map (run) 7→(φ, ext(sn)) is injective on
runs.

   Internal soundness is a property of the procedure that makes the checker redundant on
its outputs; it is what the LCF architecture of Chapter 7 achieves by construction. Trace-
faithfulness is the opposite kind of property, and realistic procedures fail it.

Example 1.10 (Independent subgoals). Let states be pairs (G, T) of a list G of open goals
and a partial derivation tree T. Let the goal be p ∧q from assumptions p, q. The rule ∧I

1.5. THE RESIDUE OF A RUN                                                  5


replaces the goal by the two subgoals p and q, and a closing rule discharges any open goal
that is an assumption. After ∧I, two runs are possible: close p first, then q, or close q first,
then p. Both end in the same final tree ∧I(hypp, hypq). The procedure has two distinct
traces with equal output, so it is not trace-faithful.


1.5  The residue of a run


Example 1.10 is almost too small to notice. At scale the phenomenon is pervasive: lemmas
tried and abandoned, orderings explored, heuristics consulted, and dead branches pruned
all appear in the trace and none appears in the output.

Definition 1.11 (Residue). Let Run(φ) be the set of runs of R on φ and ϱ : Run(φ) →D the
output map. For d ∈D the residue of d at φ is the fibre ϱ−1(d). Two runs are output-equivalent
if they lie in the same fibre.

  A downstream task that can be served by the pair (φ, d) alone must be invariant on
fibres. A task that must distinguish runs inside a fibre cannot be served by the derivation,
however carefully the derivation is checked. This is the earliest and simplest statement of
the suﬀiciency criterion that Chapter 10 generalizes: a representation is suﬀicient for a task
precisely when the task factors through it.

Proposition 1.12 (Factorization criterion). Let Run(φ)̸ = ∅and let T  : Run(φ) →Y be a
task, understood as a function of the full run (so Y̸ = ∅). There is a function T′  : D →Y with
T = T′ ◦ϱ if and only if T is constant on every fibre of ϱ.

Proof. If T = T′ ◦ϱ and ϱ(r) = ϱ(r′) then T(r) = T′(ϱ(r)) = T′(ϱ(r′)) = T(r′). Conversely,
if T is constant on fibres, define T′(d) as the common value on ϱ−1(d) when this fibre is
nonempty and arbitrarily otherwise. Then T′ ◦ϱ = T by construction.          ■


   Proposition 1.12 is a restatement of the fact that a function factors through a quotient
if and only if it respects the equivalence relation, and its simplicity is deliberate. The sub-
stance lies in applying it to tasks that people actually want served by a proof: checking,
teaching the method, adapting it to a neighbouring problem, and diagnosing a failed ap-
plication. These are not functions of d alone, and Chapter 11 shows this with explicit coun-
terexamples.


1.6  What this chapter fixes


Four points are used throughout.

   1. Assurance attaches to the checker and the translation, never to the producer (Theo-
    rem 1.5, Proposition 1.7).
   2. Absence of a derivation is not evidence of invalidity.
   3. A search procedure is a transition system, and its traces carry strictly more informa-
      tion than its outputs in general (Example 1.10).
   4. A task is served by an output exactly when it factors through the extraction map
     (Proposition 1.12).

Chapter 2

Search Spaces and Strategies




Chapter 1 treated a producer as a black box. This chapter opens it. A producer that is
a search has a space it explores, a strategy that orders the exploration, and a guarantee,
when there is one, that every derivation that exists will eventually be reached. The guar-
antee is called fairness, and the main theorem below shows that fairness is the only thing
a strategy must add to a refutationally complete calculus to obtain a semi-decision proce-
dure. The second half of the chapter records, with proofs from Church’s theorem, three
limits that no strategy escapes: there is no computable bound on derivation size, there is
no terminating completion of the search, and no combination of derivation-finding and
finite-countermodel-finding settles every statement.


2.1  Inference systems and saturation


The calculi of automated reasoning share a skeleton that is independent of the logic. Ob-
jects are generated from earlier objects by rules, and one distinguished object is contradic-
tory.

Definition 2.1 (Inference system). An inference system is a tuple I = (X, M, |=, ⊥, R) where
X is a set of objects (formulas, clauses, sequents), M is a set of models, |= ⊆M × X is a
satisfaction relation, ⊥∈X is an object satisfied by no model, and R is a set of rule instances
(Q, c) with Q ⊆X finite and c ∈X. A rule instance is sound if every model satisfying all of
Q satisfies c; I is sound if all its rule instances are.
   For N ⊆X, write m |= N if m |= x for all x ∈N, and call N unsatisfiable if no model
satisfies it. N is saturated if (Q, c) ∈R and Q ⊆N imply c ∈N. I is refutationally complete if
every saturated unsatisfiable set contains ⊥.

Definition 2.2 (Derivation, fairness). A derivation from N0 ⊆X is a sequence N0 ⊆N1 ⊆
N2 ⊆· · · in which Ni+1 \ Ni consists of conclusions of rule instances whose premises lie         S
in Ni. Put N∞=    i Ni. The derivation is fair if every rule instance (Q, c) with Q ⊆Ni for
some i has c ∈Nj for some j.

   Because premise sets are finite and the chain is increasing, Q ⊆N∞holds if and only if
Q ⊆Ni for some i. Hence fairness is exactly saturation of the limit.

Lemma 2.3 (Fairness is limit saturation). A derivation is fair if and only if N∞is saturated.

8                        CHAPTER 2. SEARCH SPACES AND STRATEGIES


Proof. Suppose the derivation is fair and (Q, c) ∈R with Q ⊆N∞. Since Q is finite and
the chain increasing, Q ⊆Ni for some i, so c ∈Nj ⊆N∞for some j. Conversely, if N∞is
saturated and Q ⊆Ni, then Q ⊆N∞so c ∈N∞, hence c ∈Nj for some j.        ■

Theorem 2.4 (Fair derivations decide refutability). Let I be sound and refutationally complete,
and let N0, N1, . . . be a fair derivation from N0. Then N0 is unsatisfiable if and only if ⊥∈Ni for
some i.

Proof. (⇐) By induction on i, every model of N0 is a model of Ni: the base case is trivial,
and for the step each new element is the conclusion of a sound rule instance with premises
in Ni, hence satisfied by every model of Ni. If ⊥∈Ni then a model of N0 would satisfy ⊥,
which no model does. So N0 is unsatisfiable.
  (⇒) Suppose N0 is unsatisfiable. Since N0 ⊆N∞, any model of N∞would be a model
of N0, so N∞is unsatisfiable. By Lemma 2.3 it is saturated, so by refutational completeness
⊥∈N∞, hence ⊥∈Ni for some i.                              ■

  The (⇒) direction is what makes search complete: if a contradiction is derivable, a fair
strategy reaches it. The (⇐) direction is soundness. Neither direction says anything about
how long the search takes, nor about what happens when N0 is satisfiable.

Corollary 2.5 (Non-refutation is silent). If N0 is satisfiable and the derivation is fair, then ⊥/∈
Ni for all i. If the derivation is stopped at a finite stage k without ⊥, then nothing follows about the
satisfiability of N0 unless Nk is saturated.

Proof. The first claim is the contrapositive of the (⇐) direction of Theorem 2.4. For the
second, a finite stage that is not saturated is a prefix of a derivation that may still produce ⊥,
so its silence is uninformative. If instead Nk is saturated and ⊥/∈Nk, then Nk is satisfiable
by the contrapositive of refutational completeness, and so is N0 ⊆Nk.          ■


2.2  Implementing fairness: the given-clause loop


Fairness is a property of an infinite derivation. A strategy must achieve it by a local rule
for choosing what to do next. The standard device is a given-clause loop, with a processed
set P and an unprocessed queue U.

Definition 2.6 (Given-clause strategy). Assume that for every finite Q ⊆X only finitely
many rule instances have premises inside Q. Fix k ≥1. Start with P0 = ∅and U0 = N0
(finite), each element stamped with its time of entry. At step t:
   1. select u ∈Ut:  if k  | t, take the element with the oldest time stamp; otherwise any
     element;
   2. set Pt+1 = Pt ∪{u};
   3. add to the queue every conclusion c of a rule instance (Q, c) with u ∈Q ⊆Pt+1 that
       is not already present, stamped t.
If Ut = ∅the loop halts.

Proposition 2.7 (The loop is fair). The derivation Nt = Pt ∪Ut produced by a given-clause
strategy is fair.

2.3. EXISTENCE VERSUS DISCOVERY                                           9


Proof. Each step adds finitely many elements by the finiteness assumption, so for each el-
ement e only finitely many elements enter before e. Let rkt(e) be the number of queue
elements older than e at time t. Newly arriving elements are younger than e and do not
increase rkt(e); at every k-th step the oldest element is removed, so while rkt(e) > 0 it
decreases by 1 at least once in every k steps. Hence e is selected within k(rkt0(e) + 1) steps
of its entry at time t0, so every element of N∞is eventually moved to P.
  Now let (Q, c) be a rule instance with Q ⊆N∞. Every element of Q is eventually pro-
cessed. Let u be the element of Q processed last, at some step t. Then Q ⊆Pt+1 and u ∈Q,
so c is added to the queue (or was already present) by step 3. Thus c ∈N∞, and N∞is
saturated. If the loop halts with U = ∅the same argument applies to the finite set N∞= P.
By Lemma 2.3 the derivation is fair.                              ■

  The role of the age-based selection is to defeat starvation. A strategy that always prefers
the element with the best heuristic score can postpone an old clause forever; the periodic
oldest-first selection is a minimal concession to fairness, and it is the reason a heuristic guid-
ing a fair loop can change the order in which derivations are found without changing which
derivations are eventually found. Chapter 15 makes this the basis of a general statement
about learned guidance.


2.3  Existence versus discovery


A transition system with a goal may have a run without any particular search finding it.
Let R = (Σ, →, ι, F, ext) be as in Definition 1.8 of Chapter 1 and call s live if there is a path
from s to F.

Proposition 2.8 (Iterative deepening finds a run when one exists). Suppose the set of suc-
cessors of a state is finite and effectively computable from the state (finite branching together with
a decidable edge relation is not enough, since it need not yield a terminating enumeration of the
successors), and that F is decidable. Let DFSL(φ) be depth-first search from ι(φ) that explores all
paths of length at most L. Then the procedure that runs DFS1, DFS2, . . . in turn halts with a run
on φ if and only if ι(φ) is live, and then returns a run of minimal length.

Proof. Finite branching makes the tree of paths of length at most L finite, so DFSL termi-
nates. If ι(φ) is live with a shortest run of length n, then DFSL fails for L < n and succeeds
for L = n, returning a run of length n. If ι(φ) is not live no DFSL succeeds and the iteration
does not halt.                                          ■

   Plain depth-first search without a bound is not complete in this sense: on a system with
an infinite path from ι(φ) that precedes the useful branch in its ordering it never returns.
The proposition also exhibits the asymmetry that Chapter 1 named: on a non-live initial
state the procedure does not halt, and cannot, without an additional argument, report that
no run exists.


2.4  Three limits

Fix a proof system S for first-order logic: Φ is the set of first-order sentences over a finite sig-
nature containing at least one binary relation symbol, Val is the set of valid sentences, and

10                        CHAPTER 2. SEARCH SPACES AND STRATEGIES


S is sound and complete with decidable Chk. Gödel’s completeness theorem guarantees
such systems exist, and we use:

Theorem 2.9 (Church 1936, Turing 1936). [CITED: CHURCH, TURING] For a signature with at
least one binary relation symbol, the set Val of valid first-order sentences is undecidable.

Proposition 2.10 (No computable bound on derivation size). There is no computable total
function f : N →N such that every valid φ has a derivation d with Chk(d, φ) and |d| ≤f(|φ|).

Proof. Suppose f exists. Given φ, compute f(|φ|), list the finitely many strings d with
|d| ≤f(|φ|), and run the decidable relation Chk on each pair (d, φ). Accept if some check
succeeds, otherwise reject.  If φ is valid then by assumption and completeness some d
within the bound passes.  If some d passes then φ is valid by soundness. This decides
Val, contradicting Theorem 2.9.                                ■

  The proposition has an immediate bearing on the theme of this book. Because no com-
putable function bounds the length of the shortest derivation, no procedure can promise
that the compressed object of Chapter 1 is small relative to the statement it certifies. The
residue discarded in extraction, or the derivation itself, may be larger than any bound one
could state in advance.

Definition 2.11 (Finite countermodel). A sentence φ has a finite countermodel if some finite
structure for the signature satisfies ¬φ. Let FM be the set of such sentences.

Proposition 2.12 (Two witnesses, two enumerations). Both Val and FM are recursively enu-
merable and disjoint.

Proof. Val is recursively enumerable by Proposition 1.2 of Chapter 1. For FM, enumerate
pairs of a finite structure and a sentence and evaluate the sentence in the structure; evalu-
ation in a finite structure is decidable. Disjointness is immediate: a structure falsifying φ
shows φ is not valid.                                      ■

Corollary 2.13 (Neither proved nor finitely refuted). Val∪FM̸ = Φ. Equivalently, there exist
sentences that are not valid and have no finite countermodel; every such sentence is rejected by every
combination of a sound derivation-finder and a sound finite-model-finder.

Proof. If Val∪FM = Φ, then given φ run the enumerations of Val and FM in parallel; exactly
one eventually produces φ, and the answer is read off. This decides Val, contradicting
Theorem 2.9.                                          ■


2.5  Outcomes of a bounded search


The proposition and corollary above justify a three-valued reading of the result of any
practical attempt on a first-order goal.

Definition 2.14 (Outcomes). An attempt on φ with a prover and a finite-model finder
returns one of
   • Proved(d) with Chk(d, φ), from which φ ∈Val follows;
   • Refuted(m) with m a finite structure and m |= ¬φ, from which φ /∈Val follows;

2.6. SUMMARY                                                              11


   • Undetermined, from which nothing follows.

  By Corollary 2.13, the third outcome cannot be eliminated by waiting longer or by
adding a finite-model finder.  It is a structural feature of first-order automated reason-
ing, and the discipline of non-certification of Chapter 1 is its operational consequence.
Chapter 12 extends this three-valued vocabulary from statements to transformations of
verified artifacts, where an analogous undetermined outcome has a different cause (leaving
a certified fragment rather than exhausting a budget) and, as we will argue, a different
meaning.


2.6  Summary


Fair strategies make refutationally complete calculi into semi-decision procedures (Theo-
rem 2.4). Fairness is implemented, not assumed, by age-based selection (Proposition 2.7).
Existence of a run and discovery of a run are different properties (Proposition 2.8). Three
barriers survive any such implementation: no bound on derivation size (Proposition 2.10),
non-termination on satisfiable inputs (Corollary 2.5), and an irreducible undetermined
region (Corollary 2.13).

Chapter 3

Resolution, Unification, and
Saturation




Resolution is the calculus on which the most influential automated provers were built, and
it is also the cleanest laboratory for the questions of this book. It has one rule, a complete-
ness proof short enough to give in full for the propositional case, and a first-order extension
whose only new ingredient is unification, which can also be proved correct from scratch.
At the end of the chapter, resolution is placed in the framework of Chapters 1 and 2: it is a
proof system, its fair saturation is a producer, and the proof extracted from a saturation is
a compression whose residue can be seen with the naked eye.



3.1  Propositional resolution


Fix a countable set A of propositional atoms. A literal is an atom p or a negated atom ¬p;
write L for the complement of L. A clause is a finite set of literals, read as their disjunction,
and the empty clause is written □. A valuation v : A →{0, 1} satisfies a clause if it makes
some member true, so □is satisfied by no valuation. A set of clauses is satisfied by v if
every member is. A clause is a tautology if it contains both p and ¬p for some p.


Definition 3.1 (Resolution rule). From clauses C ∪{p} and D ∪{¬p} infer C ∪D. The
inferred clause is the resolvent on p. Because clauses are sets, repeated literals in C ∪D
merge automatically, so no separate factoring rule is needed in the propositional case.


  Take X to be the set of clauses, M the set of valuations, ⊥= □, and R the set of rule
instances ({C ∪{p}, D ∪{¬p}}, C ∪D). This is an inference system in the sense of Defini-
tion 2.1.


Proposition 3.2 (Soundness). Every instance of the resolution rule is sound.



Proof. Let v satisfy C∪{p} and D∪{¬p}. If v(p) = 1 then v does not satisfy ¬p, so it satisfies
some member of D and hence C ∪D.  If v(p) = 0 then it does not satisfy p and satisfies
some member of C.                                       ■

3.2  Completeness by elimination


The completeness proof below eliminates one atom at a time. The elimination is the Davis–
Putnam procedure, and Chapter 5 returns to it as the ancestor of conflict-driven learning.

Lemma 3.3 (Elimination preserves satisfiability). Let N be a finite set of non-tautological
clauses and p an atom.  Split N = E ∪P ∪Q where P is the set of clauses containing p, Q
the set containing ¬p, and E the set containing neither. Let Resp(N) be the set of resolvents on p
of a clause of P with a clause of Q, and put Np = E ∪Resp(N). Then N is satisfiable if and only
if Np is satisfiable, and every clause of Np is in N or is a resolvent of two clauses of N.


Proof. The last claim is immediate from the construction. If v |= N then v satisfies every
resolvent by Proposition 3.2 and every clause of E, so v |= Np.
   Conversely, let v |= Np; we may take v arbitrary on p and modify only that value. Write
P −= {C : C ∪{p} ∈P} and Q−= {D : D ∪{¬p} ∈Q}, where C and D do not contain p
or ¬p because the clauses are non-tautological. The resolvents are exactly the clauses C ∪D
for C ∈P −, D ∈Q−.
   Case 1: some C0 ∈P −is not satisfied by v. Then for every D ∈Q−the resolvent C0 ∪D
is satisfied by v, hence v satisfies D. Let v′ agree with v except v′(p) = 1. Then v′ satisfies all
of P through p, all of Q because each D is satisfied by v and therefore by v′ (which agrees
with v off p), and all of E.
   Case 2: every C ∈P −is satisfied by v. Let v′ agree with v except v′(p) = 0. Then v′
satisfies all of Q through ¬p, all of P because every C is satisfied, and all of E.
   In either case v′ |= N.                                    ■

Theorem 3.4 (Completeness for finite sets).  If N is a finite unsatisfiable set of propositional
clauses, then □is derivable from N by finitely many resolution steps.


Proof. By induction on the number k of atoms occurring in N.
   Let N◦be N with all tautologies removed. A valuation satisfies a tautology, so N◦has
the same models as N, and a derivation from N◦is a derivation from N. So we may assume
N contains no tautologies. If □∈N there is nothing to prove, which covers k = 0: with no
atoms every clause is □, and an unsatisfiable N must contain it.
   Let k ≥1 and □/∈N, and choose an atom p occurring in N. By Lemma 3.3, Np is
finite, unsatisfiable, and mentions only atoms other than p, hence fewer than k atoms. By
the induction hypothesis, □is derivable from Np. Each clause of Np is either in N or a
resolvent of two clauses of N, so prefixing the derivation by the corresponding steps gives
a derivation of □from N.                                   ■


  To pass from finite to arbitrary sets we use the compactness theorem for propositional
logic.

Theorem 3.5 (Compactness). [CITED: GÖDEL, MAL’CEV] A set of propositional clauses is satis-
fiable if and only if every finite subset is satisfiable.

Corollary 3.6 (Refutational completeness). Propositional resolution is sound and refutationally
complete in the sense of Definition 2.1: every saturated unsatisfiable set of clauses contains □.

Proof. Let N be saturated and unsatisfiable. By compactness some finite N0 ⊆N is unsat-
isfiable. By Theorem 3.4 there is a derivation C1, . . . , Cn = □in which each Ci is in N0
or a resolvent of earlier lines. By induction on i, each Ci ∈N: lines in N0 lie in N, and a
resolvent of two members of N lies in N because N is saturated. Hence □= Cn ∈N.  ■

  Combined with Theorem 2.4, any fair derivation of resolvents from a finite set N0 of
clauses eventually contains □if and only if N0 is unsatisfiable. For propositional clauses
over finitely many atoms the closure is finite, so the procedure terminates on every input;
this is the propositional face of the dichotomy that Church’s theorem makes sharp at first
order.


3.3  Unification


First-order clauses contain variables, and the resolution rule must find substitutions that
make complementary literals equal. Fix a signature of function symbols with arities and
a countable set V of variables. Terms are built freely: a variable, or f(t1, . . . , tn) with f of
arity n. The size |t| of a term is the number of symbol occurrences. A substitution σ is a
map from variables to terms that is the identity on all but finitely many variables, extended
homomorphically to terms and written on the left. Substitutions compose as functions.
  An equation is a pair s .= t of terms. A substitution σ is a unifier of a finite set E of
equations if σ(s) = σ(t) for every (s .= t) ∈E. A unifier σ is most general if every unifier θ
of E factors as θ = θ′ ◦σ for some substitution θ′.
Definition 3.7 (Solved form). A set of equations is in solved form if it has the shape {x1 .=
t1, . . . , xm .= tm} with the xi pairwise distinct variables, none of which occurs in any tj. Its
associated substitution is σE = {xi 7→ti}.

  The following transformation rules, due to Martelli and Montanari in this form, act on
a finite set E of equations.
   • Delete: E ∪{t .= t} ⇒E.
   • Decompose: E ∪{f(s1, . . . , sn) .= f(t1, . . . , tn)} ⇒E ∪{si .= ti : 1 ≤i ≤n}.
   • Conflict: E ∪{f(. . . ) .= g(. . . )} ⇒fail if f̸ = g.
   • Orient: E ∪{t .= x} ⇒E ∪{x .= t} if t is not a variable.
   • Occurs: E ∪{x .= t} ⇒fail if x occurs in t and t̸ = x.
   • Eliminate: E ∪{x .= t} ⇒E[x 7→t] ∪{x .= t} if x /∈Var(t) and x occurs in E.
Constants are function symbols of arity zero, so Decompose with n = 0 coincides with
Delete.

Theorem 3.8 (Unification). Every sequence of applications of the rules terminates. It terminates
either in fail, in which case E has no unifier, or in a solved form E′, in which case σE′ is a most
general unifier of E.

Proof. Rules preserve unifiers. For Delete the equation is satisfied by every substitution. For
Decompose, σ(f(⃗s)) = σ(f(⃗t)) if and only if σ(si) = σ(ti) for all i, because terms are built
freely. Orient is symmetric. For Eliminate, if σ(x) = σ(t) then σ ◦{x 7→t} = σ as substitu-
tions (on x both give σ(t) = σ(x), and elsewhere both give σ(y)), so σ unifies E if and only
if it unifies E[x 7→t]. For Conflict and Occurs there is no unifier of the displayed equation:
heads differ in the first case, and in the second σ(x) = σ(t) would force a term to be a

proper subterm of itself, which contradicts finiteness of size since |σ(t)| > |σ(x)| whenever
x occurs in t̸ = x.
   Termination. Call a variable solved in E if it is the left-hand side of an equation x .= t with
x /∈Var(t) and x occurs nowhere else in E. Let n1(E) be the number of variables occurring
in E that are not solved, n2(E) the total size of all terms in E, and n3(E) the number of
equations of the form t .= x with t not a variable. We check that each rule strictly decreases
the triple (n1, n2, n3) in the lexicographic order, with n1 never increasing in the rules that
decrease n2 or n3.
   • Delete: no variable becomes unsolved (n1 does not increase) and n2 drops by 2|t| ≥2.
   • Decompose: the set of variables is unchanged; a solved variable is not in the decom-
     posed equation, so it stays solved; n2 drops by 2.
   • Orient: the variable set and n2 are unchanged; n1 does not increase; n3 drops by 1.
   • Eliminate: after the step x occurs only in x .= t and x /∈Var(t), so x is solved, whereas
     before it was not solved because it occurred elsewhere. A variable solved before re-
     mains solved:  it occurred only in its own equation, so it is neither x nor in t, and
      substituting t for x in the right-hand side of its equation cannot introduce it. Hence
     n1 decreases by at least 1.
The lexicographic order on triples of naturals is well-founded, so the rules cannot be ap-
plied forever.
  Normal forms. Suppose no rule applies and the result is not fail. Every equation has
a variable on the left, else Orient, Decompose, Conflict or Delete would apply; none is of
the form x .= x or has x in its right-hand side, else Delete or Occurs would apply; and no
left-hand variable occurs elsewhere in E, else Eliminate would apply. Thus E is in solved
form.
  Most general unifier. Let E′ = {xi .= ti} be in solved form and σ = σE′. Since no xj
occurs in any ti we have σ(ti) = ti = σ(xi), so σ unifies E′. If θ is any unifier of E′ then
θ(xi) = θ(ti), so θ ◦σ = θ on each xi and trivially elsewhere; thus θ = θ ◦σ and σ is most
general. Since the rules preserve unifiers, σ is a most general unifier of the original E. ■


3.4  First-order resolution

A first-order literal is an atomic formula P(t1, . . . , tn) or its negation, a clause a finite set of
literals with all variables implicitly universally quantified, and clauses are identified up to
renaming of variables. A structure A satisfies a clause if every assignment of the variables
into A satisfies some member.

Definition 3.9 (First-order resolution). Binary resolution: from clauses C ∪{A} and D ∪
{¬B} with no shared variables, where A, B are atoms with most general unifier σ, infer
σ(C ∪D).  Factoring: from C ∪{A, B} with A, B atoms of the same polarity and most
general unifier σ of A and B, infer σ(C ∪{A}).

Proposition 3.10 (Soundness). Binary resolution and factoring are sound: any structure satis-
fying the premises satisfies the conclusion.

Proof. Let A satisfy C∪{A} and D∪{¬B} and let a be an assignment. Define an assignment
b by b(x) = [[σ(x)]]A,a. By the substitution lemma, every term t satisfies [[t]]A,b = [[σ(t)]]A,a,
and hence the same holds for literals. Since σ(A) = σ(B), either A and B are both true

16              CHAPTER 3. RESOLUTION, UNIFICATION, AND SATURATION


under b or both false. If both true, ¬B is false under b, so D has a literal true under b, i.e.
σ(D) has a literal true under a. If both false, C has a literal true under b, i.e. σ(C) has one
under a. Either way σ(C ∪D) is satisfied under a. The argument for factoring is the same
with one premise.                                        ■

  Completeness is a consequence of two standard results about grounding, which we cite.
A ground instance of a clause is the result of replacing all its variables by closed terms.

Theorem 3.11 (Herbrand). [CITED: HERBRAND 1930, SKOLEM, GÖDEL] A set N of first-order
clauses is unsatisfiable if and only if some finite set of ground instances of members of N is unsatis-
fiable as a set of propositional clauses.

Lemma 3.12 (Lifting). [CITED: ROBINSON 1965] Let C1, C2 be clauses without shared variables,
C′1, C′2 ground instances of them, and C′ a propositional resolvent of C′1, C′2. Then there is a first-
order resolvent C of C1, C2, possibly after factoring C1 and C2, of which C′ is a ground instance.

Theorem 3.13 (Refutational completeness of resolution). First-order binary resolution with
factoring is sound and refutationally complete: if N is unsatisfiable then □is derivable from N, and
every saturated unsatisfiable N contains □.

Proof. By Theorem 3.11 there is a finite unsatisfiable set N′ of ground instances of clauses of
N. By Theorem 3.4 there is a propositional resolution derivation C′1, . . . , C′n = □from N′.
By induction on i we construct clauses Ci derivable from N by first-order resolution and
factoring such that C′i is a ground instance of Ci. If C′i ∈N′, take Ci to be the member of
N of which it is an instance. If C′i is a propositional resolvent of C′j, C′k, apply Lemma 3.12
to Cj, Ck. The only ground instance of a clause that equals □is an instance of □itself, so
Cn = □. The claim about saturated sets follows as in Corollary 3.6: every Ci lies in N by
induction.                                            ■

  Theorem 3.13 together with Theorem 2.4 gives the usual conclusion: a fair saturation
of resolvents, for instance by the given-clause loop of Proposition 2.7, is a semi-decision
procedure for unsatisfiability of first-order clause sets, and by Theorem 2.9 it cannot be
improved to a decision procedure.


3.5  Resolution as a proof system, and what extraction discards


Resolution is a proof system in the sense of Definition 1.1, a refutation system. Let Φ be the
set of finite sets of clauses, Val the unsatisfiable ones, D the set of finite sequences of clauses
annotated with their justification (an input clause, or a resolution or factoring step citing
earlier lines and a unifier), and Chk(d, N) the relation that holds when each annotation
is verified by the unification algorithm of Theorem 3.8 and the last line is □. Then Chk is
decidable, and the system is sound and complete by Proposition 3.10 and Theorem 3.13.
  The producer is a saturation. A given-clause run generates a possibly enormous set N∞
of clauses, and extraction keeps only those on which □depends.

Definition 3.14 (Proof dag). Given a run that generates □, record for each generated clause
its parents. The proof dag is the sub-dag consisting of □and all of its ancestors. The ex-
tracted derivation d is any linearization of the proof dag consistent with the parent relation.

3.5. RESOLUTION AS A PROOF SYSTEM, AND WHAT EXTRACTION DISCARDS   17


Example 3.15 (Unused material). Let N = { {p}, {¬p, q}, {¬q}, {r, s}, {¬r, s} }. A satu-
ration derives {q} from the first two clauses, □from {q} and {¬q}, and also {s} from the
last two clauses. In a run that first obtains □through {q}, the proof dag of □contains ex-
actly {p}, {¬p, q}, {¬q}, {q}, □. The clauses {r, s}, {¬r, s}, {s} are in the run and not in the
derivation. A different order of the saturation, which resolves q against ¬q before touching
the r, s clauses, yields the same derivation d with a different trace.

  Example 3.15 is tiny, but it instantiates Definition 1.11 of Chapter 1 precisely. Two runs
on the same N with different traces and the same extracted derivation share a fibre, and
the r, s clauses are part of the trace and no part of the output. Nothing in the framework
bounds the unused portion in terms of the derivation, and Proposition 2.10 shows that
even the derivation’s own size admits no computable bound in terms of the statement. A
task that depends on what was tried (for instance, which lemma candidates were found
irrelevant, which instance of a heuristic parameter produced the proof) is not a function
of d and cannot be served by it, in the sense of Proposition 1.12.

   This is not a defect of resolution. The extraction of Definition 3.14 is exactly the com-
pression a proof checker needs, and it is lossless with respect to the one task the checker
serves. The point of the book is that other tasks exist, and that the same compression is
lossy for them.

Chapter 4

Rewriting and Normalization




Rewriting is the second great engine of automated reasoning, and it differs from resolution
in a way that matters for this book. Resolution derives new facts and keeps all of them
until a contradiction appears. Rewriting replaces: a term is repeatedly simplified, the earlier
forms are discarded, and what remains is a canonical representative. A rewriting system is
thus a machine that turns a family of equal expressions into a single one, and the structure
it forgets in doing so can be stated exactly. This chapter proves the basic theory from the
ground up, namely confluence, Newman’s lemma and termination by interpretation, cites
the critical pair lemma and the correctness of completion, and ends with the observation
that a normal form is the extreme case of a compression that is suﬀicient for one task and
insuﬀicient for others.


4.1  Abstract reduction systems

An abstract reduction system is a pair (A, →) with →⊆A × A. Write →+ and →∗for the
transitive and reflexive-transitive closures, ←for the converse, and ↔∗for the equivalence
generated by →. Elements a, b are joinable, written a ↓b, if a →∗c ←∗b for some c. An
element is a normal form if no step leaves it, and b is a normal form of a if a →∗b and b is a
normal form.

Definition 4.1 (Termination and confluence). The system (A, →) is
   • terminating if there is no infinite sequence a0 →a1 →a2 →· · · ;
   • confluent if b ←∗a →∗c implies b ↓c;
   • locally confluent if b ←a →c implies b ↓c;
   • Church–Rosser if a ↔∗b implies a ↓b;
   • convergent if it is terminating and confluent.

Lemma 4.2 (Confluence is the Church–Rosser property). (A, →) is confluent if and only if it
is Church–Rosser.

Proof. (⇐) If b ←∗a →∗c then b ↔∗c, so b ↓c.
  (⇒) Suppose a ↔∗b, by induction on the length of a zigzag from a to b. Length zero
is trivial. Otherwise a ↔∗b′ by a shorter zigzag, and b′ →b or b′ ←b. By the induction
hypothesis a →∗c ←∗b′.  If b →b′ then b →b′ →∗c, so a →∗c ←∗b.  If b′ →b then
c ←∗b′ →b, and confluence gives c →∗d ←∗b, so a →∗d ←∗b.              ■

4.1. ABSTRACT REDUCTION SYSTEMS                                         19


Theorem 4.3 (Newman’s lemma, 1942). A terminating and locally confluent system is conflu-
ent.


Proof. Since the system is terminating, →+ is well-founded and we may argue by well-
founded induction. Let P(a) say that b ←∗a →∗c implies b ↓c. Assume P(a′) for every a′
with a →+ a′, and let b ←∗a →∗c. If a = b then b = a →∗c so b ↓c, and symmetrically if
a = c. Otherwise a →a1 →∗b and a →a2 →∗c, and by local confluence a1 →∗d ←∗a2.
  The induction hypothesis holds at a1 and at a2, since a →a1 and a →a2. Applying it at
a1 to b ←∗a1 →∗d gives b →∗e ←∗d. Applying it at a2 to d ←∗a2 →∗c gives d →∗f ←∗c.
Now a →a1 →∗d gives a →+ d, so the induction hypothesis holds at d, and applying it to
e ←∗d →∗f gives e →∗g ←∗f. Then b →∗e →∗g and c →∗f →∗g, so b ↓c.      ■


Corollary 4.4 (Unique normal forms). Let (A, →) be convergent. Every a ∈A has exactly one
normal form NF(a), and a ↔∗b if and only if NF(a) = NF(b). If in addition the successors of any
element are computable, then ↔∗is decidable.


Proof. A normal form exists by termination, since otherwise one could step forever. If b, c
are normal forms of a then b ←∗a →∗c, so b →∗d ←∗c by confluence; as b, c admit no
steps, b = d = c.
    If a ↔∗b then Lemma 4.2 gives a →∗e ←∗b, hence NF(a) = NF(e) = NF(b) by
uniqueness. Conversely, a →∗NF(a) = NF(b) ←∗b gives a ↔∗b. For the last claim,
compute NF(a) and NF(b) by following any sequence of steps, which halts by termination,
and compare.                                          ■


   Corollary 4.4 is the abstract content of every canonizer. Note what it does not say: all
maximal reduction sequences from a end at the same element, but nothing is claimed about
their lengths or their contents.

Proposition 4.5 (Strategy independence of the output). In a convergent system, every maxi-
mal reduction sequence from a is finite and ends at NF(a). In particular every strategy for choosing
the next step, adaptive or not, has the same output, and strategies differ only in the traces they pro-
duce.


Proof. A maximal sequence is finite by termination and ends in a normal form of a, which
is NF(a) by Corollary 4.4.                                   ■


Example 4.6 (Same output, different traces). Take rules a →b and h(x) →d(x, x) over a
signature with constants a, b, a unary h and a binary d. The rules have no overlap, and the
system is terminating. Reducing h(a) innermost gives h(a) →h(b) →d(b, b) in two steps;
reducing outermost gives h(a) →d(a, a) →d(b, a) →d(b, b) in three. The outputs coincide,
in agreement with the proposition, while both the length and the rules used differ.


   Proposition 4.5 places rewriting at the opposite pole from the search of Chapter 2. There,
strategy affects which derivation is found and whether one is found at all. Here, in a con-
vergent system, strategy affects only cost. This is the formal reason that rewriting-based
canonization is a safe component of a larger prover: it is a function, not a search.

4.2  Term rewriting and termination by interpretation

Fix a signature as in Section 3.3 of Chapter 3. A rewrite rule is a pair l →r of terms with l
not a variable and Var(r) ⊆Var(l). A term rewriting system (TRS) R is a finite set of rules.
The rewrite relation is

s →R t ⇐⇒   s|p = σ(l) and t = s[σ(r)]p for some rule l →r, position p, substitution σ,

where s|p is the subterm at position p and s[u]p is s with that subterm replaced by u.
  The most direct method for proving termination assigns each symbol a function into a
well-founded set.

Proposition 4.7 (Termination by monotone interpretation). Let each n-ary symbol f be inter-
preted by a function [f] : Nn →N that is strictly increasing in each argument. For an assignment
α : V →N define [t]α by [x]α = α(x) and [f(t1, . . . , tn)]α = [f]([t1]α, . . . , [tn]α). If [l]α > [r]α
for every rule l →r and every assignment α, then →R is terminating.

Proof. We show that s →R  t implies [s]α >  [t]α for every α. For a substitution σ and
assignment α put ασ(x) = [σ(x)]α; by induction on terms, [σ(u)]α = [u]ασ. Hence for a
step at the root, s = σ(l) and t = σ(r), we get [s]α = [l]ασ > [r]ασ = [t]α. For a step
at a deeper position, induct on the depth of p:  if s = f(s1, . . . , si, . . . , sn) and the step
takes place inside si, giving s′i with [si]α > [s′i]α, then strict monotonicity of [f] in its i-th
argument gives [s]α > [t]α. An infinite reduction s0 →s1 →· · · would give, for any fixed
α, an infinite strictly decreasing sequence [s0]α > [s1]α > · · · in N, which is impossible. ■

Example 4.8 (Addition). Let R+ consist of add(0, y) →y and add(s(x), y) →s(add(x, y)).
Put [0] = 1, [s](x) = x + 1, [add](x, y) = 2x + y. All three are strictly increasing in each
argument. For the first rule, [add(0, y)]α = 2+α(y) > α(y). For the second, [add(s(x), y)]α =
2(α(x) + 1) + α(y) = 2α(x) + α(y) + 2, which exceeds [s(add(x, y))]α = 2α(x) + α(y) + 1.
By Proposition 4.7, R+ terminates. The two left-hand sides have no overlap, so there are
no critical pairs in the sense of the next section, and R+ is convergent.


4.3  Critical pairs and local confluence


Because termination is available by Proposition 4.7 and Theorem 4.3 reduces confluence
to a local condition, what remains is to check local confluence of a TRS. The check is finite,
and it is carried out by unification.

Definition 4.9 (Critical pair). Let l1 →r1 and l2 →r2 be rules renamed to share no vari-
ables, and let p be a position of l1 such that l1|p is not a variable and unifies with l2 with
most general unifier σ. If p is the root then the two rules must not be variants of each other.
The pair
                                  ⟨σ(r1), σ(l1[r2]p) ⟩

is a critical pair. It is joinable if its two components are joinable under →R.

Lemma 4.10 (Critical pair lemma). [CITED: KNUTH–BENDIX 1970, HUET 1980] A TRS is locally
confluent if and only if all its critical pairs are joinable.

4.4. EQUATIONAL THEORIES AND COMPLETION                              21


  Because a finite TRS has finitely many critical pairs, each computed by the unification
procedure of Theorem 3.8, the lemma yields a decision procedure for confluence of termi-
nating systems.

Proposition 4.11 (Confluence of terminating TRS is decidable). There is an algorithm that,
given a finite terminating TRS, decides whether it is confluent.

Proof. Compute the finite set of critical pairs. For each pair, enumerate the reducts of each
component. In a terminating, finitely branching system the set of reducts of a term is finite:
otherwise by König’s lemma the finitely branching tree of reduction sequences would con-
tain an infinite branch, contradicting termination. So joinability is decidable by checking
whether the two finite reduct sets intersect. By Lemma 4.10, the system is locally confluent
exactly when all pairs are joinable, and by Theorem 4.3 local confluence is confluence for
terminating systems.                                      ■

Example 4.12 (Groups). Over the signature {·, −1, e} consider the ten rules

               e · x →x            x−1 · x →e  (x · y) · z →x · (y · z)
             x−1 · (x · y) →y      x · e →x    e−1 →e
               (x−1)−1 →x        x · x−1 →e  x · (x−1 · y) →y
               (x · y)−1 →y−1 · x−1

This is the classical completion of the three group axioms, due to Knuth and Bendix. Ter-
mination follows from the lexicographic path order with precedence −1 > · > e, a standard
result that we cite rather than reprove. Local confluence was checked in preparation of this
book by computing every critical pair over all ordered pairs of rules and all non-variable
positions, 55 in total, and normalizing each side: all were joinable. This is a computation
by a short independent program and has not been mechanized in a proof assistant. Grant-
ing termination, Proposition 4.11 then makes the system convergent, so by Corollary 4.4
two group terms are equal in every group if and only if they have the same normal form
(using the equational completeness theorem recalled below).


4.4  Equational theories and completion

Let E be a set of equations s ≈t between terms. The relation ↔E is the symmetric closure
of single rewrite steps using equations of E in both directions, at any position and under
any substitution, and ↔∗E is its reflexive-transitive closure. Write E |= s ≈t if every algebra
satisfying all equations of E satisfies s ≈t under every assignment.

Theorem 4.13 (Birkhoff 1935). [CITED: BIRKHOFF] E |= s ≈t if and only if s ↔∗E t.

   Birkhoff’s theorem reduces equational validity to reachability in an abstract reduction
system, so the machinery of Section 4.1 applies. If E has an equivalent presentation R in
which every equation is oriented as a rule, and R is convergent, then E |= s ≈t is decided
by comparing normal forms (Corollary 4.4). Completion searches for such an R. Given
a reduction order ≻(a well-founded order on terms closed under contexts and substitu-
tions), the Knuth–Bendix procedure maintains a pair (Ei, Ri) of unoriented equations and
oriented rules, starting from (E, ∅), using the inferences
   • Orient: move s ≈t from Ei to Ri as s →t if s ≻t (or as t →s if t ≻s);

22                       CHAPTER 4. REWRITING AND NORMALIZATION


   • Deduce: add s ≈t to Ei when ⟨s, t⟩is a critical pair of Ri;
   • Simplify: rewrite a side of an equation, or the right-hand side of a rule, by Ri;
   • Delete: remove an equation s ≈s.

Theorem 4.14 (Correctness of completion). [CITED: BACHMAIR, DERSHOWITZ, HSIANG 1986]
If a run of the procedure is fair, in the sense that every critical pair between rules that persist from
some stage onward is eventually deduced, and the run never meets an equation that is unorientable
by ≻and ends with no unoriented equations, then the limit system R∞is convergent and ↔∗R∞
coincides with ↔∗E. The procedure can fail on an unorientable equation, and can run forever.

  Completion is a fairness-governed search in the spirit of Chapter 2 (it deletes as well
as adds, so Definition 2.2 does not apply literally), and the discipline of non-certification
applies to it verbatim.  If completion fails or does not terminate, nothing follows about
the decidability of the word problem for E, which may be decidable by other means. If it
succeeds, the result is a canonizer whose assurance rests on two ingredients: termination
of R∞under ≻, and the joinability of its critical pairs, both of which a checker can verify
afterwards without trusting the run.


4.5  Normal forms as a canonical residue

Let R be convergent. The map NF  : T →T from terms to normal forms is idempotent,
sends every term to an equal term, and identifies exactly the ↔∗-equivalent terms (Corol-
lary 4.4). It is the extreme case of the compression studied in this book: a whole equiva-
lence class, together with every path inside it, is replaced by one representative.
  For a task, understood as in Proposition 1.12 of Chapter 1 as a function on the full reduc-
tion sequence rather than on its endpoint, Proposition 4.5 says that all sequences from s lie
in a single fibre of the output map.

Proposition 4.15 (What normalization serves and what it cannot). Let R be convergent and
let ϱ map a maximal reduction sequence from s to its last term.
  (i) The task “decide whether s ↔∗t” factors through ϱ.
 (ii) In Example 4.6, the task “report the number of rewrite steps used” does not factor through ϱ,
     and neither does “report whether the rule a →b was applied before h(x) →d(x, x)”.

Proof. (i) s ↔∗t if and only if NF(s) = NF(t) by Corollary 4.4, and NF(s) = ϱ(r) for every
maximal sequence r from s. So the answer is a function of the endpoints.  (ii) The two
sequences from h(a) in Example 4.6 have the same endpoint d(b, b) and different lengths,
and in the second the rule a →b is applied after h(x) →d(x, x) while in the first it is
applied before. By Proposition 1.12 neither task factors through ϱ.            ■

  The proposition is trivial to state and it carries the central message of Part I. A repre-
sentation is not suﬀicient or insuﬀicient in the abstract; it is suﬀicient for a declared task.
Normalization is suﬀicient for equality and for nothing that depends on how equality was
reached. Resolution proofs (Chapter 3) are suﬀicient for checking and for nothing that de-
pends on what was tried. Part II shows that SAT solvers, SMT solvers, and kernels exhibit
the same pattern at industrial scale, and Part III turns the pattern into a theory.

Chapter 5

SAT and Clause Learning as
Resolution with Memory




Modern propositional solvers decide satisfiability of formulas with millions of clauses, and
they do so by a procedure whose logic is almost entirely resolution. This chapter makes
the claim exact. A conflict-driven solver is a transition system whose learned clauses are
resolution consequences, so every refutation it finds is a resolution refutation, and the trace
of the search can be compressed into a certificate that an independent checker accepts. The
same material supplies the first fully worked case of a recurring theme: an optimization
that is perfectly sound for deciding satisfiability can discard exactly the information needed
to produce a model, and the discarded information can be named.


5.1  Clauses, trails, and unit propagation


Notation follows Chapter 3. A partial assignment is represented as a trail M, a finite sequence
of literals containing no complementary pair. Each element of the trail is either a decision
literal, written ld, or a propagated literal. We write M |= ¬C if for every literal l ∈C the
complement l occurs in M, and say M falsifies C. A literal is undefined in M if neither it nor
its complement occurs.
  A clause C ∪{l} is unit under M with unit literal l if M |= ¬C and l is undefined in
M. Unit propagation extends M by unit literals until no clause is unit; it refutes M against a
clause set F if some clause of F ends up falsified. A run of unit propagation is computable
in time linear in the size of F with the standard watching schemes, and the only fact we
need is that the result of propagation is well-defined as a refutation or non-refutation (it is
confluent in this sense; see Exercise 5.1).


5.2  Conflict-driven clause learning as a transition system


We follow the abstract presentation of Nieuwenhuis, Oliveras and Tinelli. A state is either
Fail or a pair ⟨M ∥F⟩of a trail and a finite set F of clauses. The initial state for a formula
F0 is ⟨ε ∥F0⟩, with the empty trail.

Definition 5.1 (Abstract CDCL). The transition rules are as follows.

     l.
Decide ⟨M ∥F⟩⇒⟨M ld ∥F⟩if l or l occurs in F and l is undefined in M.
Fail ⟨M ∥F⟩⇒Fail if M |= ¬C for some C ∈F and M contains no decision literal.

   there is a clause C′ = l′ ∪D′ such that F |= C′, M′ |= ¬D′, and l′ is undefined in M′.

  The clause C′ is called asserting:  it is unit under M′. Backjump abstracts conflict anal-
ysis, learning, and backjumping together.  It leaves the choice of C′ open except for the
requirement F |= C′; Section 5.3 shows what choices practical solvers make.

Lemma 5.2 (Invariants). Let ⟨M ∥F⟩be reachable from ⟨ε ∥F0⟩. Then
  (i) F and F0 have the same models;
  (ii) every literal l occurring in M before the first decision literal satisfies F0 |= l.


Proof. By induction on the length of the run. Both hold initially.
   (i) UnitPropagate, Decide, Fail leave F unchanged. Backjump adds C′ with F |= C′, so
F ∪{C′} and F have the same models, and these are the models of F0 by the induction

is unchanged. UnitPropagate: if M contains a decision then the new literal lies after it and
the base is unchanged; otherwise the whole of M is base, each member entailed by F0 by

each c ∈C, and F0 |= C ∪{l} by (i), so F0 |= l. Backjump: the new trail M′ l′ has M′ as a
prefix of the old trail. If M′ contains a decision, its base is the old base, and l′ lies after that
decision. Otherwise M′ is part of the old base, so each member is entailed by F0. Then
M′ |= ¬D′ gives F0 |= d for each d ∈D′, and F |= l′ ∪D′ with (i) gives F0 |= l′.     ■

falsified by M, then M satisfies F0.

by (i). A model of F0 would falsify every member of C and satisfy one, which is impossible.

every clause of F, hence by (i) it satisfies F0.                        ■

5.3. CONFLICT ANALYSIS IS RESOLUTION                                     27


   Together, Theorems 5.3 and 5.4 make the system a decision procedure for propositional
satisfiability. Notice the structure it shares with Chapter 2: soundness of the verdict does
not depend on the heuristics that drive Decide and the choice of C′, whereas termination
does depend on a non-repetition condition. This is Theorem 1.5 again.


5.3  Conflict analysis is resolution

The rule Backjump requires only F |= C′. Practical solvers choose C′ by a specific proce-
dure, and this procedure is a sequence of resolution steps. For a propagated literal l in M,
a reason for l is a clause C ∪{l} ∈F with M<l |= ¬C, where M<l is the prefix of M before l.

Definition 5.5 (Conflict analysis). Let C0 ∈F be falsified by M. For i ≥0, if Ci contains a
literal l with l a propagated literal of M, let l be the one occurring latest in M among those,
take its reason R = Di ∪{l}, and put

                             Ci+1 = (Ci \ {l}) ∪Di,

the resolvent of Ci and R on l. Stop when no such literal remains.

Proposition 5.6 (Analysis steps are resolution steps). Each Ci+1 is a resolvent of Ci and a
clause of F, so each Ci has a resolution derivation from F with at most i steps. The process terminates
after at most as many steps as M has propagated literals. Every Ci is falsified by M.

Proof. The first claim is the definition of resolution (Definition 3.1). Falsification: M |=
¬C0; if M |= ¬Ci and l is as in the definition, then M |= ¬Di is witnessed by the prefix
M<l of M, and l ∈Ci is removed, so M |= ¬Ci+1. For termination, every literal added to
Ci+1 has its complement in M<l, so strictly earlier in M than l. Hence the latest propagated
literal whose complement lies in Ci+1 is strictly earlier than l, and the sequence of literals
resolved on is strictly decreasing in trail position; each propagated literal is used at most
once.                                               ■

  The standard stopping criterion (first unique implication point) halts the process at a
clause that is falsified by M and contains exactly one literal assigned at the current decision
level; this is asserting after backjumping to the second-highest level occurring in it. We do
not need the criterion to state the following consequence.

Theorem 5.7 (CDCL refutations are resolution refutations). Suppose a run from ⟨ε ∥F0⟩
reaches Fail and every clause added by Backjump is the last or an intermediate clause Ci of a conflict
analysis as in Definition 5.5, started at a falsified clause of the current F. Then F0 has a resolution
refutation in which every added clause is a line, and the total number of resolution steps is at mostP
   j |Mj|, where Mj ranges over the trails at the conflicts that occurred.

Proof. By induction along the run, every clause in F has a resolution derivation from F0:
initial clauses trivially, and each clause added by Backjump by Proposition 5.6, whose
premises are clauses of the current F. At the final Fail, M has no decision, so every lit-
eral of M is propagated and has a reason. Let C0 be the falsified clause. Running the
analysis of Definition 5.5 until no propagated literal remains, with no decision literal to
block it, leaves a clause Cn with no literals at all: every literal c ∈Cn would have c ∈M
propagated, and so would be resolved away. Hence Cn = □. The step count follows from
the proposition.                                         ■

5.4  Certificates: RUP, RAT, and DRAT


A solver that answers “satisfiable” hands back an assignment, which any one can check
against the formula in linear time. A solver that answers “unsatisfiable” owes a proof, and
the proofs that matter in practice are logs of learned clauses.

Definition 5.10 (RUP). Let F be a clause set. A clause C has the reverse unit propagation
property with respect to F, written F ⊢1 C, if unit propagation starting from the trail
consisting of the complements l for l ∈C, as propagated literals, refutes the clause set F.

Proposition 5.11 (RUP is sound). If F ⊢1 C then F |= C.

Proof. Suppose v |= F and v̸ |= C, so v makes every l with l ∈C true, and v satisfies every
initial trail literal. Unit propagation adds a literal l only from a clause C′ ∪{l} ∈F whose
other literals are false in the current trail. By induction on the length of propagation, v
satisfies every literal of the trail:  if v satisfies all literals in the trail, then v |= c for each
c ∈C′, and since v |= C′ ∪{l} we get v |= l. So v satisfies the trail. A refutation produces
a clause of F all of whose literals are false under the trail, hence under v, contradicting
v |= F.                                              ■

Definition 5.12 (RUP refutation, checker). A RUP refutation of F is a sequence of clauses
C1, . . . , Cn with Cn = □such that F ∪{C1, . . . , Ci−1} ⊢1 Ci for each i. The relation
ChkRUP(d, F) holds when d is a RUP refutation of F; it is decidable in polynomial time,
by running unit propagation for each line.

Theorem 5.13 (RUP is a complete proof system). The system with Φ the finite clause sets, D
the finite sequences of clauses, ChkRUP as above, and Val the unsatisfiable clause sets is sound and
complete.

Proof. Soundness follows from Proposition 5.11 by induction on i: every Ci is entailed by
F, so □is entailed, so F is unsatisfiable.

5.4. CERTIFICATES: RUP, RAT, AND DRAT                                      29


   For completeness let F be unsatisfiable over atoms p1, . . . , pn. For 0 ≤k ≤n call a clause
k-full if it contains, for each 1 ≤j ≤k, exactly one of pj, ¬pj, and no other literals. The
n-full clauses each exclude exactly one total assignment. Each n-full clause C is RUP with
respect to F: the trail C is a total assignment, and since F is unsatisfiable it falsifies a clause
of F, so propagation refutes immediately. List all 2n n-full clauses. Having listed all (k+1)-
full clauses, each k-full clause C is RUP with respect to them: from the trail C, the clause
C ∪{pk+1} is unit and propagates pk+1, after which the clause C ∪{¬pk+1} is falsified. List
the k-full clauses next. Continuing down to k = 0 lists □. This is a RUP refutation.   ■

  The proof is, of course, exponentially long in n. Its role is to show that RUP is not weaker
than resolution in provability, while the actual strength in terms of proof size is that of the
clause sequences produced by solvers, which are polynomial in the number of learned
clauses (each clause learned by the analysis of Definition 5.5 is RUP; see Exercise 5.2).

   Certificates in practice permit one further kind of line, whose soundness is subtler and
instructive.

Definition 5.14 (RAT). Let F be a clause set, C a clause and l ∈C a literal. C has the
resolution asymmetric tautology property with respect to F on l if for every D ∈F with
l ∈D, the resolvent (C \ {l}) ∪(D \ {l}) satisfies F ⊢1 (·) (or is a tautology).

Proposition 5.15 (RAT preserves satisfiability, not entailment).  If C is RAT with respect to
F on l, and F is satisfiable, then F ∪{C} is satisfiable. In general F̸ |= C.

Proof. Let v |= F. If v |= C we are done. Otherwise let v′ agree with v except v′(l) = 1,
so v′ |= C. Let D ∈F.  If l /∈D, then v′ |= D, since v |= D and only the value of l
changed in the direction that cannot falsify a clause not containing l. If l ∈D, the resolvent
R = (C \ {l}) ∪(D \ {l}) is entailed by F (it is RUP, hence entailed by Proposition 5.11, or
it is a tautology), so v |= R. Since v̸ |= C, we have v̸ |= C \ {l}, hence v |= D \ {l}, and the
same literals are true under v′ because v′ differs from v only on the atom of l, which does
not occur in D \ {l} unless the clause is tautological. So v′ |= D. Thus v′ |= F ∪{C}.
   For the failure of entailment take F = {{q}} and C = {p} with l = p: no clause of F
contains ¬p, so C is RAT on p, and F̸ |= {p}.                         ■

  A DRAT proof is a sequence of steps each of which adds a clause that is RUP or RAT
with respect to the current database, or deletes a clause from the current database, and
ends with an addition of □.

Theorem 5.16 (DRAT checking is sound). If d is a DRAT proof for F0, then F0 is unsatisfiable.

Proof. Let DB0 = F0 and DBi+1 the database after step i + 1. We claim DBi is satisfiable
whenever F0 is. By induction: an RUP addition C satisfies DBi |= C by Proposition 5.11,
so DBi ∪{C} has the same models as DBi. An RAT addition preserves satisfiability by
Proposition 5.15. A deletion gives a subset, which is satisfiable if DBi is. If F0 is satisfiable
then the final database is satisfiable; but it contains □, which no assignment satisfies. Hence
F0 is unsatisfiable.                                       ■

  Theorem 5.16 deserves emphasis because it shows how little a certificate need certify.
The intermediate lines of a DRAT proof need not be consequences of F0, and a deletion
step may weaken what later steps are checked against. What the checker certifies is a single

5.5  Elimination, and what a reduced formula forgets


Chapter 3 introduced elimination of an atom p by Davis and Putnam, which replaces N by
Np. Practical solvers use it as bounded variable elimination during preprocessing, and the
transformation is sound for satisfiability by Lemma 3.3. It is not an equivalence-preserving
transformation: N |= Np, but Np̸ |= N in general, and models of Np are not models of N
until a value for p is supplied.

Proposition 5.17 (Model reconstruction). Let N = E ∪P ∪Q be as in Lemma 3.3, with
P −= {C : C ∪{p} ∈P}. If v |= Np, define v′ to agree with v off p and put v′(p) = 1 if v falsifies
some member of P −, and v′(p) = 0 otherwise. Then v′ |= N.

Proof. This is the pair of cases in the proof of Lemma 3.3.                  ■

  The reconstruction rule reads the eliminated clauses P (and Q is not needed).  It is a
function of v and of P, so a task that asks for a model of the original formula N is not
determined by the reduced formula alone. A single example makes this precise.

Example 5.18 (Same reduced formula, opposite extensions). Let N1 = {{p, a}, {¬p, b}}
and N2 = {{p, b}, {¬p, a}}. Eliminating p gives, in both cases, (Ni)p = {{a, b}}. The valua-
tion v with v(a) = 1, v(b) = 0 satisfies {a, b}. To extend v to a model of N1 we need ¬p ∨b
true with b false, so p = 0. To extend it to a model of N2 we need p ∨b true with b false, so
p = 1. The same reduced formula and the same model of it demand opposite values of p.

  Example 5.18 instantiates Proposition 1.12 exactly. Consider the task “produce a model
of the original formula”, and let the fibre over a reduced formula consist of all originals that
reduce to it. The task is not constant on the fibre, so it does not factor through the reduction.
Practical solvers respond by retaining a reconstruction stack, the eliminated clauses in order,
which is precisely the residue that Proposition 5.17 requires. Decision (satisfiable or not)
factors through the reduction; model production does not; and the stack is the minimal
supplement that restores it.


5.6  The residue of a solver run


The pieces assemble into a description of what a SAT result consists of, and of what it
discards.
   • A satisfiable verdict is certified by a total assignment, which is checkable in linear time
     and carries no information about the search.
   • An unsatisfiable verdict is certified by a DRAT proof, whose lines are not necessarily
     consequences of the input (Theorem 5.16). The proof certifies the verdict and noth-
     ing about the decisions, heuristic scores, restarts, or clause deletions of the run that
     produced it, nor about preprocessing steps that were later undone by reconstruction.
   • Different runs, with different decision orders, yield different proofs of the same ver-
       dict. The verdict is the common output of a large fibre of runs (Definition 1.11).

Chapter 6

Theories, Congruence, and
Combination




Propositional search proves facts about Boolean structure. Most of the questions asked of
automated provers in verification, planning, and scientific computing involve arithmetic,
equality, arrays, and data types, and the solvers that answer them are propositional solvers
wrapped around decision procedures for theories. The wrapping is logically simple, since
it amounts to adding theory lemmas to a resolution proof, but its consequences for what a
certificate means are substantial. A certificate now has two parts, a Boolean skeleton and
a collection of theory facts, each checked by a different mechanism, and the correctness
of the whole depends on the agreement of each mechanism with the intended meaning
of the theory. This chapter proves correctness for the three components that matter for
certificates: the lazy architecture, congruence closure for equality, and Farkas certificates
for linear arithmetic; it states the combination theorem of Nelson and Oppen and proves
the half of it that explains its hypothesis.


6.1  Theories and the lazy architecture


Definition 6.1 (Theory, T-validity). A theory T is a class of structures over a signature Σ
(its models), closed under isomorphism. A formula is T-valid, written |=T φ, if every model
of T satisfies it under every assignment, and T-satisfiable if some model of T and some
assignment satisfy it. A T-lemma is a T-valid clause of ground literals.

  A quantifier-free formula in conjunctive normal form over Σ-atoms is a set of clauses
whose atoms are Σ-literals (equalities, inequalities, applications of predicate symbols).
The Boolean abstraction replaces each distinct atom by a propositional variable.  The
lazy architecture couples the CDCL system of Chapter 5 to a procedure that decides
T-satisfiability of conjunctions of literals.

Definition 6.2 (DPLL(T)). The rules are those of Definition 5.1 with one addition, in which

  M.
Backjump as before, with the side condition F |=T C′ in place of F |= C′.
