remaining cases are verbatim. At Fail the argument of Theorem 5.3 shows that F0 |=T c for
every c ∈C and F0 |=T C, which no T-model can satisfy. The second claim follows from
Theorem 5.7, regarding each member of L as an additional input clause: the analysis uses
only clauses of the current F, which consists of F0, members of L, and clauses learned by
resolution.                                            ■

  Theorem 6.3 gives the shape of a certificate for a theory-unsatisfiable result: a resolution
(or RUP) refutation from F0 ∪L, together with a proof for each member of L that it is T-
valid. The first part is checked as in Chapter 5. The second part is where theory-specific
certificate formats enter.


6.2  Equality: congruence closure


The theory EUF of equality with uninterpreted functions has as models all structures for
a signature of function symbols (constants being 0-ary symbols). A ground term is a term
without variables, where free variables are treated as constants. Let S be a finite set of
ground terms closed under subterms and E ⊆S × S a set of equations.

Definition 6.4 (Congruence closure). The congruence closure of E on S is the smallest equiv-
alence relation ≡on S such that E ⊆≡and, whenever f(s1, . . . , sn), f(t1, . . . , tn) ∈S with
si ≡ti for all i, we have f(s1, . . . , sn) ≡f(t1, . . . , tn).

Theorem 6.5 (Correctness of congruence closure). For s, t ∈S: E |=EUF s ≈t if and only if
s ≡t. Consequently a conjunction E ∧V j sj̸ ≈tj with all terms in S is EUF-unsatisfiable if and
only if sj ≡tj for some j.

Proof. (⇐) We show every pair of ≡is entailed by E by induction on the generation of ≡as
a closure: the pairs of E are entailed; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of = are sound;
and congruence is sound, since in any structure equal arguments give equal values of f.
  (⇒) Suppose  s̸ ≡t.  Build a structure A with domain S/≡.  For an n-ary symbol
f and classes c1, . . . , cn:  if there are representatives ti ∈ci with f(t1, . . . , tn) ∈S, put
fA(c1, . . . , cn) = [f(t1, . . . , tn)]; otherwise put fA(c1, . . . , cn) = c0 for a fixed class c0. The
first clause is well defined: if ti, t′i ∈ci and both f(⃗t), f(⃗t′) ∈S then ti ≡t′i, so f(⃗t) ≡f(⃗t′)
by the congruence clause. By induction on terms in S, which is subterm-closed, [[u]]A = [u]
for every u ∈S. Hence A satisfies every equation of E (as its sides are ≡) and falsifies
s ≈t because [s]̸ = [t]. So E̸ |= s ≈t.

34              CHAPTER 6. THEORIES, CONGRUENCE, AND COMBINATION


   For the consequence: if some sj ≡tj then E |= sj ≈tj contradicts the disequality, so
the conjunction is unsatisfiable. If no sj ≡tj then A satisfies E and every disequality. ■

Proposition 6.6 (The merging algorithm). Start from the identity relation on S. Repeat: merge
the classes of s, t for some (s ≈t) ∈E with s̸ ≡t, or for some f(⃗s), f(⃗t) ∈S with si ≡ti for all
i and f(⃗s)̸ ≡f(⃗t). This halts after at most |S| −1 merges, and the final relation is the congruence
closure.

Proof. Each merge reduces the number of classes by one, so at most |S| −1 merges occur.
At the end no merge is applicable, so the relation contains E and is closed under congru-
ence; hence it contains the congruence closure. Conversely, by induction on the number
of merges performed, each merged pair belongs to the congruence closure, since it follows
from E and congruence from pairs already in the closure. So the final relation equals it. ■


  With union-find and a signature table the algorithm runs in time O(n log n) (cited:
Downey, Sethi, Tarjan 1980). For certificates the important feature is that the algorithm
can record why each merge occurred, either because of an input equation or because of
congruence on earlier merges. The record is a derivation in the equational calculus with
rules for hypotheses, reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and congruence, and the checking
relation for such derivations is a simple tree check.

Proposition 6.7 (Equality lemmas have checkable explanations). If a congruence closure com-
putation derives sj ≡tj then it yields a subset E′ ⊆E and a derivation of sj ≈tj from E′ in the                 W
equational calculus, and the clause   e∈E′ ¬e ∨sj ≈tj is an EUF-lemma.

Proof. Associate with each merge the set of input equations used in its justification, which
is finite and defined by recursion on the order of merges. The derivation is assembled from
the recorded justifications, and soundness of the calculus rules gives E′ |= sj ≈tj, so the
clause is valid.                                         ■

Example 6.8 (Explanations are not unique). Let E = {a ≈b, b ≈c, a ≈c}. Both E′ =
{a ≈c} and E′′ = {a ≈b, b ≈c} explain a ≈c. A run that processes the third equation
first records E′, and one that processes the first two records E′′. Both are valid lemmas.
They yield different clauses in the Boolean engine and so different subsequent behavior,
with the same verdict.


6.3  Linear arithmetic: Farkas certificates


For linear arithmetic over the rationals the natural lemma certificate is a nonnegative com-
bination of the inequalities that contradicts itself. Let A ∈Qm×n and b ∈Qm.

Proposition 6.9 (Farkas certificates are sound).  If y ∈Qm satisfies y ≥0, y⊤A = 0 and
y⊤b < 0, then the system Ax ≤b has no solution x ∈Qn.

Proof. If Ax ≤b and y ≥0 then y⊤Ax ≤y⊤b. But y⊤Ax = 0 and y⊤b < 0, giving 0 < 0. ■

Theorem 6.10 (Farkas’ lemma). [CITED: FARKAS 1902] The system Ax ≤b over Q is unsatisfi-
able if and only if there is y ≥0 with y⊤A = 0 and y⊤b < 0.

6.4. COMBINING THEORIES                                                  35


   Together these make the Farkas vector y a complete certificate for the linear-rational
theory LRA (non-strict case), checkable in exact rational arithmetic by one matrix-vector
multiplication. The checker is tiny and the certificate says nothing about how it was found:
simplex pivots, bound propagation, and branching on disequalities are all absent from it.
For linear integer arithmetic no certificate with comparable simplicity is complete in the
same way, because deciding integer feasibility is NP-hard and the certificates involve cuts
and case splits, whose format we do not develop here.

Remark 6.11 (Exactness). A certificate y is a rational vector and the check is an equation
in Q. A solver that finds y in floating point is free to do so; the check, however, must be
exact. A claim certified with floating-point arithmetic is a different claim, about a different
structure. This is the first appearance of the translation of Section 1.3 of Chapter 1 in the
context of theories, where the choice of the structure (rationals, integers with unbounded
range, machine integers with overflow, floating-point numbers) is the content of τ.


6.4  Combining theories


Real problems mix theories. The classical method of Nelson and Oppen combines decision
procedures for theories T1, T2 over disjoint signatures, first purifying a formula so that each
literal belongs to one signature (introducing fresh variables for foreign subterms), and then
exchanging equalities among the shared variables.

Definition 6.12 (Stably infinite, arrangement). A theory T  is stably infinite if every T-
satisfiable quantifier-free formula is satisfiable in an infinite model of T. Let V be a finite
set of variables. An arrangement of V  is an equivalence relation on V ; write δ∼for the
conjunction of the equalities x = y for x ∼y and the disequalities x̸ = y for x̸ ∼y.

Theorem 6.13 (Nelson–Oppen). [CITED: NELSON AND OPPEN 1979; TINELLI AND HARANDI
1996] Let T1, T2 be stably infinite theories over disjoint signatures, φ1, φ2 conjunctions of literals
over Σ1 and Σ2 respectively, and V the set of variables occurring in both. Then φ1 ∧φ2 is satisfiable
in T1∪T2 if and only if there is an arrangement ∼of V such that φi∧δ∼is Ti-satisfiable for i = 1, 2.

  The direction (⇒) holds without any hypothesis and has a one-line proof: a model of
T1 ∪T2 satisfying φ1 ∧φ2 determines the arrangement x ∼y iff x, y have equal values, and
each reduct is a model of Ti satisfying φi ∧δ∼. The direction (⇐) is where stable infinity
is used: given models A1, A2 satisfying the two parts, one uses the Löwenheim–Skolem
theorem and stable infinity to make both of the same infinite cardinality, builds a bijection
between their domains that respects the arrangement on V , and transports one structure
along the bijection to form a model of the union. The next example shows the hypothesis
cannot be dropped.

Example 6.14 (Stable infinity is necessary). Let T1 over the empty signature (equality only)
have as its models exactly the structures with exactly two elements. T1 is not stably infinite.
Let T2 = EUF over a signature {f}. Take φ2 = f(x)̸ ≈f(y) ∧f(y)̸ ≈f(z) ∧f(x)̸ ≈f(z)
and φ1 the empty conjunction. Then V = ∅since φ1 mentions no variables, so the unique
arrangement is the empty relation. The formula φ1 is T1-satisfiable and φ2 is T2-satisfiable.
Nevertheless φ1 ∧φ2 is unsatisfiable in T1 ∪T2: in every model there are exactly two ele-
ments, while φ2 requires three pairwise distinct values f(x), f(y), f(z). The combination
procedure would answer satisfiable, which is wrong, and the error is silent.

36              CHAPTER 6. THEORIES, CONGRUENCE, AND COMBINATION


  The example is a concrete instance of the discipline that runs through this book. A
procedure’s verdict is correct relative to hypotheses about its inputs (here, stable infinity),
and a certificate that does not carry those hypotheses can be valid in the checker’s sense
and misleading in the user’s.


6.5  Certificates for theory results and the growth of the trusted
    base


Combining the pieces: an SMT unsatisfiability result is certified by a resolution proof
over the Boolean abstraction together with a certificate for each theory lemma (Theo-
rem 6.3). The checker for the whole is the union of checkers: a clause-level proof checker,
a derivation checker for EUF lemmas (Proposition 6.7), an exact-arithmetic checker for
LRA (Proposition 6.9), and so on for each theory.

Theorem 6.15 (Soundness of the combined checker). Let Chkres be a sound checker for reso-
lution refutations, and for each theory Ti let ChkTi be a sound checker for Ti-lemmas, in the sense
that ChkTi(c, C) implies |=Ti C. Define ChkSMT((⃗c, d), F) to hold if d is a resolution refutation
of F ∪{C1, . . . , Ck} and ChkTij (cj, Cj) for each j. Suppose in addition that every clause valid in
some Ti is valid in the combined theory T (the models of T are structures whose reducts to each
component signature are models of that component). Then ChkSMT((⃗c, d), F) implies that F is
unsatisfiable in T.

Proof. A model of T and an assignment satisfying F would satisfy each Cj, which is T-
valid by the additional hypothesis and the soundness of ChkTij . It would therefore satisfy
all of F ∪{C1, . . . , Ck}, contradicting the soundness of the resolution refutation.    ■

  The additional hypothesis is not automatic.  It is exactly what fails if a component is
stated for a different structure than the one the combined problem intends. The trusted
base therefore grows with each theory, and in two ways: the checker for each theory must
be trusted, and the intended structure of each theory must be correctly described. The second
is the translation of Proposition 1.7 again.

Remark 6.16 (Quantifiers and the third outcome). Solvers also accept quantified formulas,
and treat quantifiers by instantiation. A refutation found this way is certified by the in-
stances used, which are ground and so fall under the preceding theorem. A failure to find
a refutation is not a model: it supports only the answer unknown. The three-valued out-
come of Definition 2.14 appears here for the same reason as in first-order logic, and the
discipline of non-certification forbids reading unknown as satisfiable.


6.6  What an SMT result discards


The structure of the residue is now visible in miniature. A result is a Boolean skeleton plus
lemmas, and discarded are: the order of theory conflicts; which of several valid explana-
tions was chosen (Example 6.8); how a Farkas vector was found; the arrangement guesses
made during combination; and, for quantified input, which instantiations were tried and
abandoned. None of this affects the soundness of the verdict. A task that depends on any
of it, for instance diagnosing why a verification condition failed to prove, or porting a proof

6.6. WHAT AN SMT RESULT DISCARDS                                        37


to a slightly different theory, cannot be served by the certificate alone. Chapter 7 turns to
the case where the certificate is checked by a small kernel and the same questions arise at
the level of tactics and proof terms.

Chapter 7

Kernels, Tactics, and the Trusted Base




The previous chapters concerned procedures whose outputs are certificates for an inde-
pendent checker. This chapter concerns the architecture in which the checker is built into
the interface: a small kernel guards the only way to construct a theorem, and arbitrary pro-
grams, called tactics, may drive the kernel as they please. The architecture, due to Milner
and his collaborators in the LCF system, is the reason the soundness of a large body of
machine-checked mathematics reduces to the correctness of a few thousand lines of code.
This chapter states that reduction precisely, extends it to dependent type theory with proof
irrelevance, and examines three things it leaves open: whether the theorem proved is the
one intended, which axioms the proof actually uses, and what the kernel’s identification
of proofs forgets.


7.1  The LCF discipline

Definition 7.1 (Kernel). A kernel for a set Φ of statements with semantic validity Val ⊆Φ
consists of an abstract type Thm, a function concl : Thm →Φ, and a finite set of rules. Each
rule is a partial function r : Thmk × Args ⇀Thm. The only way to obtain a value of type
Thm is to apply a rule to arguments (the abstraction barrier). The kernel is locally sound if
for every rule r and arguments θ1, . . . , θk, a with concl(θi) ∈Val for all i and r(⃗θ, a) = θ
defined, we have concl(θ) ∈Val.

  The abstraction barrier is not a mathematical notion; it is enforced by the type system
of the implementation language, by module opacity in ML or by the checker of the proof
assistant in more modern systems. Granting it, the following holds for arbitrary client
programs.

Theorem 7.2 (Soundness for arbitrary clients). Let K be a locally sound kernel and P any
program, with any control flow, any use of heuristics or randomness, and possibly nonterminating,
that interacts with K only through its interface. If P evaluates to a value θ : Thm in some execution,
then concl(θ) ∈Val.

Proof. Every value of type Thm that exists in an execution was created by some rule ap-
plication, since the abstraction barrier forbids any other construction. By induction on the
number of rule applications that precede the creation of a given value, each existing value
has a valid conclusion: the arguments to a rule application are earlier values, hence valid

                                      38

7.2. DEPENDENT TYPE THEORY AS KERNEL                                   39


by the induction hypothesis (or are non-Thm data, which are unconstrained), and local
soundness gives validity of the result.                            ■

  Theorem 7.2 is Theorem 1.5 of Chapter 1 in a different dress. The producer is a program
and the checker is distributed into the constructors of Thm, but the structure is the same:
assurance depends on the kernel and on nothing else. A program that fails to produce a
Thm value says nothing.

Definition 7.3 (Tactic). A tactic is a function t from goals g ∈Φ to pairs t(g) = (⃗g, v) where⃗
g = (g1, . . . , gk) is a list of subgoals and v : Thmk →Thm is a validation. The tactic is valid
if for every goal g, with t(g) =  (⃗g, v), and every⃗θ with concl(θi) = gi, the value v(⃗θ) is
defined and concl(v(⃗θ)) = g.

  A tactic proof of g with a family of tactics resolves the subgoals recursively: solve(g) =
v(solve(g1), . . . , solve(gk)) for t(g) = (⃗g, v) and a tactic t chosen for each goal; a goal for
which the chosen tactic returns the empty list of subgoals is closed by v().

Proposition 7.4 (Valid tactics prove what they say).  If every tactic used is valid and solve(g)
terminates, then concl(solve(g)) = g.  If some tactic is not valid, then solve(g), if it terminates,
still has a valid conclusion by Theorem 7.2, but concl(solve(g)) may differ from g.

Proof. The first claim is by induction on the recursion depth of solve: each solve(gi) has
conclusion gi by hypothesis, so validity of the tactic at g gives concl(v(. . .)) = g. The second
is Theorem 7.2. For a tactic that is not valid, take t(g) = ((), v) with v() a theorem whose
conclusion is some valid h̸ = g.                                ■

  The proposition separates two guarantees that are often conflated. A bug in a tactic can-
not produce an invalid theorem, but can produce a valid theorem about the wrong statement. The
defense in practice is that the client states g and compares it with concl(θ) at the end, or in a
dependently typed system that the kernel checks a proof term against a stated type; either
way the agreement of the statement is checked, and that check is a separate component of
the trusted base (Section 7.5).


7.2  Dependent type theory as kernel

Modern proof assistants of the Lean family replace the abstract type Thm by the typing
judgement of a dependent type theory, with the Curry–Howard reading in which a propo-
sition φ is a type and a proof is a term of that type. The proof system of Definition 1.1 is
then:

   • Φ is the set of types in a given environment of declarations,
   • D is the set of terms,
   • Chk(d, φ) holds when the kernel’s type checking derives d  : φ in the environment,
     and
   • Val is truth in an intended interpretation of the type theory.

Soundness is the consistency and correctness of the type theory with respect to a model;
completeness fails by Gödel’s incompleteness theorem for the theories at issue and is not
expected. The decidability of Chk is a hypothesis of Definition 1.1 that holds for strongly
normalizing theories. The metatheory of the type theories implemented by real kernels,

40                CHAPTER 7. KERNELS, TACTICS, AND THE TRUSTED BASE


which add features such as proof irrelevance, quotients, and primitive literals, is subtler
than the textbook case, and the question of how closely the implemented checker matches
the idealized rules has been studied in detail; we treat decidability and soundness of the
kernel as hypotheses and do not rederive them (see Carneiro 2024 for a careful analysis of
the Lean kernel).

  Three features of the Lean kernel matter for this book.
  (i) Proof irrelevance. Any two proofs of the same proposition (a term of a type living in
     the universe Prop) are definitionally equal.
 (ii) Axioms are declarations. Besides definitions and theorems, an environment may con-
      tain axioms: constants with a type and no value. Lean’s standard library uses three,
      propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and the elaborator, a trusted-for-convenience
     but untrusted-for-soundness component, can add a distinguished axiom sorryAx as
     a placeholder for incomplete work.
 (iii) Elaboration is separate from checking. Tactics and the elaborator build terms; the kernel
     checks the final terms. By the argument of Theorem 7.2, bugs in the elaborator cannot
     produce an invalid theorem. They can produce a term whose type is not the one the
     author intended.


7.3  Proof irrelevance as a collapse

Let φ : Prop and let Proof(φ) be the set of closed terms of type φ in some environment.

Proposition 7.5 (No term distinguishes proofs). Let π1, π2 ∈Proof(φ). Then π1 ≡π2 by
definitional equality. Consequently, for every term f of function type ( h : φ) →B in the kernel,
f π1 ≡f π2, and in particular no definable function from proofs of φ to a data type separates π1
from π2.


Proof. The first claim is the proof irrelevance rule. The second follows because definitional
equality is a congruence: the application f πi is built from πi, and ≡is closed under ap-
plication. Two definitionally equal terms of a data type are indistinguishable by any term,
since any observation is again a term and congruence applies.               ■


  The proposition states, as a theorem, the way in which the kernel is a quotient. All proofs
of a proposition are mapped to a single point, and the structure internal to a proof, namely
which lemmas it used, which case split it chose, and how long it is, is invisible from inside
the system. This is a deliberate and valuable design choice. It makes checking cheaper, since
equality of proofs need never be tested, and it keeps data from depending on proofs. In the
vocabulary of Chapter 1, the kernel realizes the factorization criterion (Proposition 1.12) as
an architectural principle: the only tasks permitted on proofs are those that factor through
the single class.

  The proof term itself, however, is an ordinary data structure outside the kernel, available
to meta-level programs, and these can read what the kernel refuses to distinguish. This is
the first appearance of a fact that organizes Part III: the residue is not destroyed by the
collapse, it is relocated, and whether it is retained depends on whether anyone keeps the
term.

7.4. AXIOM FOOTPRINTS                                                     41

7.4  Axiom footprints


A proof term mentions constants, each constant has a type and possibly a value mentioning
further constants. The dependency closure cl(c) of a constant c is the smallest set containing c
and every constant occurring in the type or value of a member of cl(c). The axiom footprint
Ax(c) is the set of axiom constants in cl(c).

Proposition 7.6 (Locality of checking). Let Γ be a well-formed environment and c : φ a decla-
ration in it. The sub-environment Γc consisting of the members of cl(c), in their original order, is
well-formed and c : φ is derivable in it. Consequently φ is derivable in the pure type theory extended
by exactly the axioms of Ax(c) and the definitions in cl(c).

Proof. Inspection of the typing and reduction rules shows that checking a declaration con-
sults only the constants occurring in it and those whose definitions are unfolded during
conversion; unfolding a constant reveals its value, whose constants lie in the closure by
definition. Hence the check of each declaration in cl(c) succeeds in Γc exactly as in Γ, by
induction along the declaration order. This is a property of the kernel’s design and is as-
sumed here.                                           ■

  The proposition says that the footprint is the logical cost of a theorem: it identifies the
additional principles that were assumed in order to establish c. Two warnings follow from
earlier chapters.

Proposition 7.7 (Footprint is not a function of the statement or the definitional class). There
are two proofs π1, π2 of the same proposition φ, definitionally equal by proof irrelevance, with
Ax(π1)̸ = Ax(π2).

Proof. Let φ be the proposition 2 + 2 = 4 over the natural numbers. The term π1 =  rfl
depends on no axioms. Let π2 be the term obtained by proving φ via excluded middle,
case analysis on φ ∨¬φ using Classical.em; its closure contains Classical.choice. Both have
type φ : Prop, so π1 ≡π2 by Proposition 7.5. Their footprints differ.            ■

  The proposition has a consequence that is easy to miss. Since the footprint is a prop-
erty of the term and not of the definitional class, a statement of the form “the theorem is
choice-free” is a claim about a particular term and must be established by inspecting that
term, for instance by a footprint audit of the final environment. It cannot be read off from
the statement of the theorem, and it is not preserved if the kernel replaces a proof by a
definitionally equal one.

Proposition 7.8 (The placeholder axiom is inconsistent). The constant sorryAx has a type of
the form ∀(α : Sort u), α (with an additional Boolean flag distinguishing synthetic placeholders).
Hence every proposition φ has a term sorryAx φ of type φ whose footprint contains sorryAx. A
theorem whose footprint contains sorryAx therefore certifies nothing beyond the Boolean fact that
the file compiled with warnings.

Proof. Instantiate the type at α = φ.                              ■

  The elaborator inserts sorryAx not only for an explicit placeholder but also as error re-
covery when elaboration of a declaration fails, so that later declarations can be elaborated
against it. The practical consequence, which was found in the experiments underlying

42                CHAPTER 7. KERNELS, TACTICS, AND THE TRUSTED BASE


the verification-inheritance papers of the author’s corpus, is that the presence of a stored
value for a declaration is not evidence of successful verification: the check that matters is
the footprint, computed on the final environment, which must exclude sorryAx.


Example 7.9 (An axiom that encodes the compiler). The decision procedures decide and
native_decide both establish decidable propositions by evaluation. The first has the kernel
itself reduce a decision procedure to true, so its footprint is the footprint of the procedure.
The second evaluates the procedure with the compiled evaluator and records the result
through an axiom, Lean.ofReduceBool, whose soundness is the correctness of the compiler
and its runtime. Its footprint therefore contains an axiom with no model-theoretic content,
whose justification is the correctness of a code generator. Both procedures produce a term
of the same type; they differ in what they ask the reader to trust.



7.5  The trusted base of a verified statement


Gathering the components identified in this and the preceding chapters, the assurance
attached to a declaration c : φ depends on the following list, and on nothing else.


Definition 7.10 (Trusted base). The trusted base of a verified result c : φ consists of

(T1) the kernel implementation and the soundness of its type theory with respect to the
     intended interpretation;
(T2) the axioms in Ax(c), each read at its intended meaning (and including any axiom,
     such as Lean.ofReduceBool, that encodes a trusted program);
(T3) the definitions in cl(c) that appear in φ, as faithful formalizations of the notions they
     name; and
(T4) the translation τ from the intended claim ψ to φ (Definition 1.6).


   Items (T1) and (T2) are the traditional focus of discussions of the trusted base and are
the part addressed by re-checkers and footprint audits. Items (T3) and (T4) are specifica-
tions, and no kernel checks them. A theorem about a quantity named jerk in a formalized
mechanics is a theorem about the formal definition. Whether the definition captures the
physical or mathematical notion is an extra-kernel obligation, which is the subject of Chap-
ter 9.


Proposition 7.11 (Assurance decomposition). Suppose (T1) holds, the axioms in Ax(c) are
true in the intended interpretation, the definitions in cl(c) interpret as intended, and τ is adequate.
Then the intended claim ψ is true.  If any of these hypotheses fails, no conclusion about ψ follows
from c : φ.



Proof. Soundness of the kernel gives φ ∈Val relative to the interpretation, which by hy-
pothesis validates the axioms and definitions. Adequacy of τ gives ψ by Proposition 1.7.
The last sentence records that nothing in the premises substitutes for a failed hypothesis.
Example 6.14 shows a verdict going wrong when a hypothesis of a procedure fails silently,
and Example 7.9 shows the trusted base growing by an axiom that encodes a program. ■

7.6. SCRIPTS AND TERMS                                                    43

7.6  Scripts and terms


A tactic script is a history, a sequence of commands that, run in the elaborator, produces a
term. The elaboration map from scripts to terms is a many-to-one function, so scripts and
terms are related exactly as search traces and derivations were in Chapter 1.

Proposition 7.12 (Scripts are not recoverable from terms). Let Elab map scripts to the terms
they produce. In general Elab is not injective: there are distinct scripts producing the same term, and
a script’s structure (the decomposition into lemmas, the order of independent subgoals, comments)
is not determined by the term.

Proof. For a goal p∧q with hypotheses p, q, the scripts that close the two conjuncts in either
order both produce the same term ∧I hp hq, as in Example 1.10. Comments and layout do
not affect the term at all.                                    ■

  Consequently the three layers of a machine-checked result, the script, the term, and the
proposition proved, are linked by two many-to-one maps, and each map is a collapse in
the sense that will be made precise in Part III. The term is the right object for the kernel, the
script is the right object for a human who wants to understand, adapt, or repair the proof,
and the proposition is the right object for the reader of the result. A representation fixed
at one layer is suﬀicient for the tasks of that layer and, in general, for no others.

Chapter 8

Certificates and Checkers




Chapters 5 to 7 met certificates in three forms: logs of learned clauses, theory lemmas with
their explanations, and terms checked by a kernel. This chapter abstracts what they share.
A certifying computation returns an answer together with a witness that a simple, indepen-
dent procedure can check; the witness is bound to a particular input; and the checker’s
correctness, not the producer’s, carries the assurance. After the abstract definition, the
chapter treats the case that is not a single call but a pipeline of transformations, where a
certificate for the last stage must be connected to the original input; proves the asymmetry
between certifying unsatisfiability and certifying satisfiability through a pipeline; and de-
scribes the third architecture for a checker, proof by reflection, in which the certificate is
the input itself and all of the content lies in a verified computation.



8.1  Certifying computation


Definition 8.1 (Certificate scheme). Let R ⊆X × Y be a relation between inputs and
answers, to be read as “y is a correct answer for x”. A certificate scheme for R consists of a
set W of witnesses and a decidable relation Wit ⊆X × Y × W such that
  (i) (soundness) Wit(x, y, w) implies R(x, y), and
  (ii) (completeness) R(x, y) implies Wit(x, y, w) for some w.
A certifying algorithm for R computes, from x, a pair (y, w);  its output is accepted  if
Wit(x, y, w).


Theorem 8.2 (Assurance rests on the checker). If (x, y, w) is accepted, then R(x, y), whatever
algorithm computed (y, w).  If R(x, y) then there exists some witness accepted, but no particular
algorithm is guaranteed to find it.

8.3  Proof by reflection


The certificates described so far are objects that a checker examines. A different architecture
runs the decision procedure inside the checker. Suppose a kernel can evaluate functions
and has a theorem relating a Boolean-valued function A : X →Bool to a property P:

                         sound : ∀x, A(x) = true →P(x).

Definition 8.7 (Reflective proof). The reflective proof  of P(x0) is the term π(x0) =
sound x0 rfl.

  The kernel accepts π(x0)  : P(x0) exactly when it can verify that the argument rfl  :
A(x0) = true typechecks, that is, when it reduces A(x0) to true by computation.

Theorem 8.8 (Size and cost of reflective proofs). Assume sound is a theorem accepted by the
kernel. Then π(x0) has size |x0| + O(1) plus the size of a reference to sound, independent of the
running time of A. The kernel’s checking cost is the cost of reducing A(x0).  If π(x0) is accepted,
then P(x0) holds in every interpretation validating the kernel.

Proof. The term consists of one constant, one argument x0, and the constant rfl. Acceptance
requires the type of rfl, which is A(x0) = A(x0), to be convertible with A(x0) = true, which
holds if and only if A(x0) and true are definitionally equal, that is, if A(x0) reduces to true.
Soundness of the kernel gives the last claim.                         ■

8.4. HOW LARGE MUST CERTIFICATES BE?                                    47


   Reflective proofs invert the usual trade-off: the certificate is tiny, the check is expensive,
and the correctness argument has moved into the proof of sound, which is done once. They
are also the extreme case of a trace-free certificate. The proof term contains nothing that
depends on how A reached its answer, and the reduction performed by the kernel is not
recorded. A reader who asks why P(x0) holds is told to rerun the computation. This will
become the example of an object that is suﬀicient for checking and minimally informative
for diagnosis, in the sense made precise in Chapter 10.

  A variant evaluates A(x0) with a compiled evaluator outside the kernel and records
the outcome through an axiom (Example 7.9). The proof term is the same and the cost
drops, at the price of replacing the kernel’s reduction by trust in the compiler. The footprint
(Definition of Section 7.4) is where the difference appears.


8.4 How large must certificates be?


Certificate size is a resource in its own right. For propositional logic the question has a
famous formulation.

Theorem 8.9 (Cook and Reckhow 1979). [CITED: COOK AND RECKHOW] There is a propositional
proof system, in the sense of Definition 1.1 restricted to propositional tautologies and polynomial-
time Chk, in which every tautology has a proof of polynomial size in the size of the tautology, if and
only if NP = co-NP.

   This sits beside Proposition 2.10, which showed that for first-order logic no computable
bound exists. For propositional logic, bounds exist for each fixed system (Haken’s theo-
rem, Theorem 5.9, shows exponential lower bounds for resolution), and the existence of
a system with polynomial bounds for all tautologies is equivalent to an open question of
complexity theory. Whatever the answer, the shape of the situation is that of the first chap-
ter: a certificate scheme is a compression of the evidence, and the compressed object can
be large.

   Verified checkers for the standard clausal certificate formats have been built inside
proof assistants (Cruz-Filipe, Heule, Hunt, Kaufmann, Schneider-Kamp 2017; Tan, Heule,
Myreen 2021), so that for propositional unsatisfiability the chain from certificate to mean-
ing can be mechanized end to end, leaving the encoding of the user’s problem as the
remaining item of the trusted base.


8.5  Certificates are bound to inputs


A witness certifies R(x, y) for the particular x it was checked against. Two features follow,
and Chapter 12 builds on both.

Proposition 8.10 (Fragility of binding). In general Wit(x, y, w) does not imply Wit(x′, y, w) for
an instance x′ equivalent to x in meaning. Even an alphabetic renaming of variables may invalidate
a literal-clause proof.

Proof. A DRAT proof refers to variables by number. Let F = {{1, 2}, {¬1}, {¬2}} with the
proof consisting of the lines {2} and □: the line {2} is RUP, since assuming ¬2 makes
{1, 2} unit, propagating 1 and falsifying {¬1}. Rename variable 2 to 3 to obtain F ′ =

{{1, 3}, {¬1}, {¬3}}, equivalent to F up to renaming. The same proof fails on F ′: the line
{2} is not RUP, because assuming ¬2 propagates nothing.                 ■

  The certificate’s validity is a fact about a syntactic pair, and its meaning (the semantic
claim it supports) is a fact about the pair’s interpretation. The two can come apart when
an artifact is transformed. An analogous point holds for proof terms against statements: a
term checked against a type is checked against that exact type up to definitional equality,
not up to logical equivalence.


8.6  Certificates are not explanations


By Theorem 8.2, any two witnesses for the same (x, y) serve the acceptance task equally.
This is both the strength of certificates and the reason they cannot serve every purpose.
Consider tasks that depend on the witness itself: finding the shortest witness, finding the
witness that uses a given lemma, locating which input clauses a witness never touches,
adapting a witness to a perturbed input. These are functions of w, not of (x, y), and by
Proposition 1.12 none of them factors through the acceptance relation. The consequence
for later chapters is stated here in its simplest form.

Proposition 8.11 (Acceptance is invariant on witnesses). Let w1, w2 be two witnesses with
Wit(x, y, w1) and Wit(x, y, w2). Any task that depends on the acceptance of (x, y, w) alone gives
the same result for w1 and w2. A task with T(w1)̸ = T(w2) is not determined by acceptance.

Proof. The first sentence is the definition of a task depending on acceptance only; the second
is its contrapositive.                                      ■

tasks, of which checking is one, and that the right question about any representation is
which members of the family it is suﬀicient for.

Chapter 9

Verification Obligations




Part II ended with a checked derivation and a list of what the check leaves out: the trans-
lation from the intended claim, the meaning of the definitions, the structure of the search.
This chapter begins the construction of a framework for the second half of that list, where
what is at stake is not whether a proof is correct but whether a correct proof supports the use
that is made of it. In the sciences the use is a claim about a physical or empirical system,
and three questions can then be asked of a machine-checked result separately: whether the
mathematics is right, whether the mathematical model respects the principles the science
takes for granted, and whether the model corresponds to what is measured. The questions
are independent, in a sense that can be made exact, and the three answers need different
kinds of evidence. The chapter defines a verified result as a structured object, proves the
independence, gives one of the obligations (dimensional consistency) a complete formal
treatment, and introduces the ledger in which an honest report records which obligations
are discharged by what.


9.1 A verified result is a tuple


Definition 9.1 (Bridged result). A bridged result consists of
  (i) a proof system S (Definition 1.1) and a formal theorem φ ∈Φ with a checked derivation
       d, Chk(d, φ);
  (ii) a class M of models (mathematical objects, such as dynamical systems or structures)
      of which φ is a statement;
 (iii) a class P of target systems (physical, computational, or empirical) together with a
      bridge β  : P ⇀M assigning to each target system within its scope S = dom(β) an
      idealizing model, under stated bridge hypotheses;
 (iv) an observation protocol ν specifying, for each target system p ∈S, which operations
     produce data and how data are compared with the values of model quantities, with
     a stated error model; and
 (v) an empirical claim ψ about target systems in S, asserted to follow from φ together with
      the bridge hypotheses.

  The tuple makes explicit what Proposition 1.7 left implicit. The kernel certifies (i) alone.
Everything else is an obligation of a different kind. Their separation has a precise form.

Definition 9.2 (Three obligation layers). For a bridged result,

(O2) compatibility with principles: every model in M satisfies the principles declared
    for the science in question (dimensional homogeneity, conservation laws, symmetries,
    causality), each stated as a predicate Πj on models;
(O3) correspondence: for every p ∈S the model β(p) predicts the values given by the pro-
    tocol ν within the declared tolerance, and the conditions under which this prediction
    is counted as success or failure were fixed before the data were collected.

  The layers are logically independent: no two imply the third.

Proposition 9.3 (Independence of the layers). For each choice of a layer there is a bridged result
satisfying the other two and failing that one.

Proof. We give a one-line witness for each; the second and third are developed in the ex-

conjecture with no proof: the relation E = mc2 before any derivation from the premises of
a theory, stated as a theorem of a formal system with a missing proof. Here Chk(d, φ) fails
for every d available, while the model satisfies the principles and agrees with measurement.

statement about a sum of a length and a time whose truth changes with units, which by

and applied where drag cannot be neglected.                        ■

isfiability, and strong in what it forbids: no verification of one layer, however thorough,
discharges another. In particular, a machine-checked proof is about O1 only.

An honest report of a verified result lists its obligations and, for each, the evidence that

and a status in

failure is localized to the layer where it occurred. A report that does not separate the layers
invites the opposite inference, that the failure of the claim undermines the proof or that
the proof secures the claim.

Chapter 10

Suﬀiciency of Certificates




Chapter 1 showed that a task is served by a representation exactly when it is constant on the
fibres of the extraction map (Proposition 1.12). That statement is true of any function, and
its content in the present setting depends entirely on which tasks are in play. This chapter
makes the dependence precise. A task family is declared, suﬀiciency is defined relative to
it, and the resulting structure is shown to be a Galois connection on the partition lattice of
the set of histories. Three consequences follow: a minimal suﬀicient representation exists
and is unique up to isomorphism; suﬀiciency has a quantitative lower bound in cardinality
and in entropy; and no representation that identifies two distinct histories is suﬀicient for
every task. The last statement is the formal core of the claim that a verified result cannot
be both maximally compressed and maximally reusable.


10.1  Histories, representations and task families


Definition 10.1 (Setting). A history space is a nonempty set H. A representation is a function
σ : H →R. A task with codomain Y is a function f  : H →Y . A task family is a set F of
tasks, with codomains allowed to vary. The kernel of a function g on H is the equivalence
relation ker g = {(h, h′) ∈H2 : g(h) = g(h′)}.

   In the application, H is the set of complete runs of a search procedure on a goal (the set
Run(φ) of Chapter 1), and the canonical representation is the extraction map ϱ : Run(φ) →
D to the checked derivation. The abstraction is nevertheless useful because the same def-
initions apply to the obligation ledgers of Chapter 9, to proof terms modulo definitional
equality (Chapter 7), and to normal forms (Chapter 4).

Definition 10.2 (Suﬀiciency). A representation σ : H →R is f-suﬀicient if there is f′ : R →
Y with f = f′ ◦σ, and F-suﬀicient if it is f-suﬀicient for every f ∈F.

  By Proposition 1.12, σ is f-suﬀicient if and only if ker σ ⊆ker f. The family enters
through a single relation.

Theorem 10.4 (Suﬀiciency is refinement). A representation σ is F-suﬀicient if and only if
ker σ ⊆ker F. Consequently:
  (i) the quotient map qF : H →H/ ker F is F-suﬀicient;
 (ii) every F-suﬀicient σ factors qF, that is, qF = u ◦σ for a unique u : σ(H) →H/ ker F; and
 (iii)  if F ⊆F′ then every F′-suﬀicient representation is F-suﬀicient.
Proof. If σ is F-suﬀicient then ker σ ⊆ker f for every f ∈F, hence ker σ ⊆T f ker f.
Conversely, if ker σ ⊆ker F ⊆ker f, Proposition 1.12 gives suﬀiciency for f. For (i),
ker qF = ker F. For (ii), define u(σ(h)) = [h]F; this is well defined because σ(h) = σ(h′)
implies (h, h′) ∈ker σ ⊆ker F, and it is unique because σ is onto σ(H). For (iii), ker F′ ⊆
ker F.                                              ■

  Theorem 10.4(ii) says that qF is the minimal suﬀicient representation:  it retains exactly
the distinctions the family can detect and no others, and every suﬀicient representation
retains at least these. The set of F-suﬀicient kernels is the down-set of the partition lattice
Π(H) generated by ker F, ordered by refinement. In particular it is closed under common
refinement (meet in the refinement order) and under passage to finer partitions, and it is
not closed under coarsening beyond ker F.

Example 10.5 (A derivation as a representation). Let H consist of runs h = (d, A) where d
is a checked derivation of a fixed goal and A ⊆{1, . . . , k} is the set of indices of alternative

Fchk = {h 7→Chk(d, φ)} the kernel ker Fchk identifies all runs with the same d, so σ is
suﬀicient and indeed minimal. For the family Fref = {h 7→[i ∈A] : 1 ≤i ≤k} the kernel
is {((d, A), (d′, A′)) : A = A′}, which σ does not refine whenever there are two runs with
equal d and different A. Each of the 2k subsets A is a separate class of ker Fref, so a suﬀicient
representation for Fref has at least 2k values (Theorem 10.10).

Extending a representation to a larger family

A result is certified once, against a family declared at the time. Later uses enlarge the family,
and the question is what the cheapest extension is.

Proposition 10.9 (Cheapest extension). Let σ be F-suﬀicient and let F′ be a further family.
Among representations τ that are F′-suﬀicient and that serve every task served by σ (that is,
Serv(σ) ⊆Serv(τ)), the coarsest has kernel ker σ ∩ker F′, and its number of values is at most
|σ(H)| · |⟨F′⟩(H)|.

Proof. The condition Serv(σ) ⊆Serv(τ) holds if and only if ker τ ⊆ker σ: the implication
from right to left is immediate, and for the converse take the task σ itself, which lies in
Serv(σ) and so in Serv(τ), giving ker τ ⊆ker σ. Together with ker τ ⊆ker F′ this gives
ker τ ⊆ker σ ∩ker F′, and the quotient by this intersection satisfies both conditions. The
classes of ker σ ∩ker F′ are the nonempty intersections of a class of ker σ with a class of
ker F′, whence the bound.                                   ■

  The extension is the pairing ⟨σ, ⟨F′⟩⟩restricted to its image. Nothing cheaper is available,
and the bound is generally not attained: whenever the new tasks are partly determined by
σ the number of classes is smaller. When the new family is a function of old data, ker σ ⊆
ker F′, the extension has no cost.

10.4 No free suﬀiciency


The preceding results are meaningful only if some tasks are not served by compressed
representations. The next theorem makes that unconditional.

Theorem 10.12 (No free suﬀiciency). Let σ : H →R. The following are equivalent.
  (i) σ is injective.
  (ii) σ is F-suﬀicient for the family Fall of all functions H →{0, 1}.
 (iii) σ is F-suﬀicient for the family Fpt = {1{h} : h ∈H} of point indicators.
In particular, if σ identifies two distinct histories then there is a task, indeed a {0, 1}-valued one,
that σ does not serve.

Proof. (i)⇒(ii): if σ is injective, any f factors as f ◦σ−1 on the image and arbitrarily else-
where. (ii)⇒(iii) is trivial since Fpt ⊆Fall. (iii)⇒(i): suppose σ(h) = σ(h′) with h̸ = h′.
Then 1{h}(h) = 1̸ = 0 = 1{h}(h′), so ker σ̸ ⊆ker 1{h}.                    ■

Corollary 10.13 (Compression is a bet on a family). Every non-injective representation of the
runs of a search procedure is suﬀicient for some declared families and insuﬀicient for others. The

families under the order by kernel inclusion.

10.5  Proof irrelevance as a suﬀiciency statement


Chapter 7 noted that proof irrelevance in a type theory with a proof-irrelevant sort of propo-
sitions collapses all proofs of the same proposition. The language of this chapter turns that
observation into a theorem about which tasks survive.

Definition 10.14 (Proof-irrelevant representation). Let H be a set of pairs (P, p) of a propo-
sition P and a proof term p of P (up to definitional equality). The proof-irrelevant represen-
tation is π(P, p) = P.

Proposition 10.15 (Tasks served by proof irrelevance). A task f is π-suﬀicient if and only
if f(P, p) = f(P, p′) for all (P, p), (P, p′) ∈H, that is, if and only if its answer depends on the
proposition alone. In particular:

  (i) type checking of any term that mentions the proof only through its type is π-suﬀicient;
  (ii) the task “return the algorithm encoded by p” is not π-suﬀicient whenever two proofs of some
    P encode different algorithms;
 (iii) the task “does p use the axiom a” is not π-suﬀicient in general, so axiom footprints are not an
      invariant of the proposition.

Proof. The first statement is Proposition 1.12 for π. For (i), a term of the form c P p is typed
by the type of p alone, by the definition of the typing rule for a proof-irrelevant argument.
For (ii) and (iii), let P have proofs p, p′ with different footprints; Chapter 7 gives such
pairs, for instance a proof that uses classical choice and one that does not. The task is
non-constant on the fibre over P.                               ■

   This is the precise sense in which proof irrelevance is an admissible collapse for depen-
dents that consume a theorem by its statement and an inadmissible collapse for any proce-
dure that must recover what was done. It is not that one is correct and the other wrong;
they are tasks with different kernels, and the declared family decides.


10.6 A geometric instance: exterior data and hidden material


The abstract statements of this chapter have a concrete instance in which the extraction

a marked part of the sheet; the question is what that restriction fixes about the rest.

Definition 10.16 (Marking problem). Let Σ ⊂R2 be a compact convex set with nonempty
interior, the sheet. A marking is a compact set A = A1 ∪· · · ∪Ak ⊂Σ with the Ai pairwise

Chapter 11

History, Stability and Repair




Chapter 10 fixed a history space and asked which tasks a representation serves. Reuse of
a verified result is rarely a task on a fixed history space: a hypothesis is strengthened, a
constant is changed, a lemma is renamed, a library is upgraded. Each is a map from one
problem instance to another, and the question becomes what a certificate says about the
instance it was not issued for. This chapter treats that question in three settings where
the answer can be computed exactly: linear arithmetic, where a certificate has a geometric
stability region; propositional clause sets, where a certificate has a combinatorial one; and
local repair of proof terms, where the relevant structure is a metric. A relational version of
the factorization criterion handles tasks with many correct outputs, and a locality theorem
shows that no representation which identifies two distant proofs can support local repair.

11.3  Clause sets: regions are up-sets


For propositional clause sets, the natural change is addition or removal of clauses. Fix

Lemma 11.7 (Unit propagation is monotone). Let G ⊆G′ be clause sets and T a set of literals.
If some maximal unit propagation sequence from T on G ends in a conflict, then every maximal
unit propagation sequence from T on G′ ends in a conflict.

11.5  Scripts are functions, terms are points


Proof assistants distinguish a script, a sequence of tactic invocations, from the term it elab-
orates to (Chapter 7). The distinction is, in the terminology of this chapter, the distinction
between a family of certificates indexed by goals and one member of the family.

Definition 11.17 (Script). Let G be a set of goals. A script is a partial computable function
s : G ⇀D. It is correct at g if s(g) is defined and Chk(s(g), g). Its region is Reg(s) = {g ∈G :
s is correct at g}.

Proposition 11.18 (Terms are points). Suppose the checking relation has unique types: Chk(t, g)
and Chk(t, g′) imply g ≡g′, where ≡is the definitional equality of the calculus. Then for every
term t, Reg(t) ⊆[g]≡for any g ∈Reg(t), that is, the region of a term is contained in a single
definitional class of goals, while the region of a script can be infinite and can contain goals pairwise
not definitionally equal.

  A script therefore carries a program for producing certificates and its region is the domain
on which that program is correct. The kernel stores one value of the program. The two have
different stability properties: a term is stable under changes to the surrounding context that
preserve its type, and a script is stable under changes that preserve its elaboration, which
depend on the version of the tactic library and not on the goal alone. These are different
kernels on different history spaces, and neither contains the other. A statement that a proof
is “robust” is therefore incomplete until it says on which of these spaces the perturbations
are taken.


11.6  What this chapter fixes


 A certificate is a region, a verdict is a point. (1) In linear arithmetic the region of a
  Farkas certificate is an open half-space, determined by the certificate’s direction, and
  the verdict region is a finite union of such half-spaces (Theorems 11.2 and 11.6). (2) A
  certificate’s perturbation margin is explicit and the best certificate attains the true ra-
  dius, but a solver need not output it (Proposition 11.4, Theorem 11.5). (3) In clause sets,
 RUP refutations are monotone under adding clauses, the verdict region is a union of
  principal up-sets, and verdict-equal refutations can have incomparable regions (Propo-
  sition 11.8, Theorem 11.10, Example 11.11). (4) Repair is a relation, and a σ-repair func-
  tion exists iff the acceptable repairs of the histories in each fibre have a common element
  (Theorem 11.13); local repair is impossible from any representation that identifies two
  distant artifacts (Theorem 11.15).

Chapter 12

Inheritance along Transformations




Results are not used where they were proved. A theorem is invoked inside a larger devel-
opment; a formula is simplified before it is handed to a solver; a formal statement is read
as a statement about a physical system. Each of these is a transformation, and each raises
the same question: what does the transformed object inherit from the verified original?
This chapter separates three things that are routinely conflated under the word “inherit”.
Validity is whether a checker accepts the transformed object. Trust is which principles the
acceptance rests on. Correspondence is whether the transformed object still says what the
original was meant to say. The three have different logics. Validity is decidable and gov-
erned by the structure of the checker (Sections 12.3 and 12.4); correspondence is undecid-
able in general and can be certified only on declared fragments (Sections 12.1 and 12.2);
trust propagates along a different graph from validity (Proposition 12.17).


12.1  Correspondence under rewriting is undecidable

Let ΦFO be the set of sentences of first-order logic over a fixed countable signature contain-
ing at least one binary relation symbol, and let φ ≡ψ mean that φ and ψ have the same
models.

Definition 12.1 (Preservation predicate). A transformation is a computable function R  :
ΦFO →ΦFO (a rewrite pass, given as a program). The preservation predicate is

                             Pres(R, φ) ⇐⇒φ ≡R(φ).

  A transformation that fails Pres at φ changes the meaning of φ; one that passes preserves
it. The predicate is the simplest formal shadow of the correspondence predicate of Chap-

required.

Theorem 12.2 (Undecidability of preservation). There is a fixed computable transformation
R⊤for which {φ : Pres(R⊤, φ)} is undecidable. Hence there is no algorithm that, given a transfor-
mation (as a program) and a sentence, decides Pres.

Proof. Let R⊤(φ) = ⊤, the constantly true sentence ∀x (x = x). Then Pres(R⊤, φ) holds iff
φ ≡⊤, that is, iff φ is valid. By Church’s theorem (Chapter 2, Proposition 2.10), validity
of first-order sentences over a signature with a binary relation symbol is undecidable. ■

accepts a preservation certificate for (R, φ) only if φ ≡R(φ), and a decidable relation ChkN
accepts a separation certificate only if φ̸ ≡R(φ). The fragment is complete if Ev is total on
such arguments.


  The verdict function Vd(R, φ) attached to the fragment has three values:
   • PRESERVED, if R ∈R, φ, R(φ) ∈F and Ev(R, φ) is a preservation certificate ac-
     cepted by ChkP;
   • NOT_PRESERVED_UNDER_R, if the same hypotheses hold with a separation cer-
       tificate accepted by ChkN;
   • OUTSIDE_CERTIFIED_FRAGMENT otherwise.

Theorem 12.6 (Soundness and non-collapse of the verdict). For every certified fragment:
  (i) Vd(R, φ) = PRESERVED implies Pres(R, φ).
  (ii) Vd(R, φ) = NOT_PRESERVED_UNDER_R implies ¬Pres(R, φ).
 (iii) Vd(R, φ) = OUTSIDE_CERTIFIED_FRAGMENT implies nothing about Pres(R, φ):
       there are fragments and arguments with this value for which Pres holds and others for which
         it fails.
If the fragment is complete then Vd is two-valued on R × F restricted to R(φ) ∈F.


Proof. (i) and (ii) are the soundness of ChkP and ChkN.   For  (iii), take the frag-
ment with F =   ∅:   it  is a certified fragment vacuously, Vd  is everywhere OUT-
SIDE_CERTIFIED_FRAGMENT, and the argument (R⊤, ⊤) has Pres true while (R⊤, ⊥)
has it false. The last statement is the definition of completeness.              ■

Theorem 12.7 (Completeness fails for full first-order logic). Let (F, R, Ev) be a certified
fragment with R⊤∈R and F = ΦFO. Then Ev(R⊤, ·) fails to return a certificate on infinitely
many sentences. In particular the fragment is not complete, and the verdict takes the third value
infinitely often.

Proof. Suppose Ev(R⊤, φ) returned a certificate for all but finitely many φ. Validity of φ
could then be decided by consulting a finite table for the exceptions and otherwise running
Ev and checking the certificate with ChkP (valid) or ChkN (not valid). This contradicts
Theorem 12.2.                                          ■

  Complete fragments exist when the underlying equivalence problem is decidable. Two
examples follow, one deliberately minimal and one of practical interest.

Example 12.8 (Conjunctions modulo associativity, commutativity and idempotence). Let
F be the set of finite nonempty conjunctions pi1 ∧· · · ∧pir of propositional atoms, with
repetitions and order allowed, regarded as formulas over the atoms. Each is equivalent to
the conjunction over its atom set at(φ), by associativity, commutativity and idempotence of
∧. Let R be the computable maps R with R(F) ⊆F.
   Claim. φ ≡ψ iff at(φ) = at(ψ).
    If the sets are equal the formulas have the same models. Conversely if p ∈at(φ) \ at(ψ)
then the assignment that makes the atoms of ψ true and all others false satisfies ψ but not
φ; symmetrically for at(ψ) \ at(φ).

  Take as preservation certificate the equality of the two atom sets, and as separation
certificate an atom lying in exactly one of them together with the assignment above.
Both are checked by a terminating computation, and Ev is total, so the fragment is
complete.  For R(φ) = φ ∧φ the verdict is PRESERVED; for R(φ) = φ ∧q with
q  /∈at(φ)  it is NOT_PRESERVED_UNDER_R; for a φ containing a disjunction  it is
OUTSIDE_CERTIFIED_FRAGMENT, whatever R does.

Example 12.9 (Propositional formulas with refutation certificates). Let F be all proposi-
tional formulas and R all computable maps preserving F. The equivalence φ ≡R(φ) holds
iff the formula ¬(φ ↔R(φ)) is unsatisfiable, a SAT instance via the Tseitin transformation
(equisatisfiable [CITED: TSEITIN 1968]). A preservation certificate is a DRAT refutation of
the Tseitin clause set (Chapter 5), a separation certificate is a satisfying assignment, which
is checked by evaluating both formulas. The fragment is complete, since SAT is decidable,
although the certificates may be exponentially large (Theorem 5.9).

  The fragment is declared before the transformation is applied, and the verdict is per
pair (R, φ), not per transformation: the same pass R is PRESERVED at some formulas and
NOT_PRESERVED_UNDER_R at others. Consistent with the discipline of Chapter 1, an
OUTSIDE_CERTIFIED_FRAGMENT verdict is never reported as a failure and never as a

≡on the types of a calculus, as in Chapter 4, so that by Corollary 4.4 A ≡B iff NF(A) =

and that Chk(t, P) holds iff ty(t) ≡P.

Example 12.11 (Addition by recursion on the second argument). Let R′+ consist of

overlap, so there are no critical pairs and R′+ is convergent. For a variable n:
   • plus(n, 0) →n, so NF(plus(n, 0)) = n = NF(n) and plus(n, 0) ≡n;

12.4  Typed dependency edges and the interface lemma


A development is an environment Γ, a finite list of constants, each an axiom (a type only),
a definition (a type and a value, transparent to conversion) or a theorem (a type and a value,
opaque to conversion). This is the structure of Chapter 7.

Convention 12.12 (Kernel discipline). The checker is assumed to satisfy the following de-
sign properties, which hold for the kernels considered in Chapter 7 and are not proved
here:

(K1) Checking a constant c consults, for each constant e occurring in the derivation, the
     type of e, and the value of e only if e is a definition that conversion unfolds.
(K2) Conversion never unfolds a theorem.

Definition 12.13 (Typed dependency edges). For constants c, e of Γ:
   • c →sem e if e occurs in the type of c (a semantic edge);
   • c →int e if e is a theorem occurring in the value of c (an interface edge);
   • c →prf e if e is a non-theorem constant occurring in the value of c (a proof-term edge).
The flat graph is the union of the three relations with their labels forgotten.

Definition 12.14 (Consulted set). The consulted set Cons(c) is the smallest set of constants
such that
 (a)  if c →e for any of the three edge kinds then e ∈Cons(c);
 (b)  if e ∈Cons(c) and e →sem e′ then e′ ∈Cons(c);
  (c)  if e ∈Cons(c) is a definition and e →prf e′ or e →int e′ then e′ ∈Cons(c).


   In words: from the declaration being checked, any dependency is followed; from a con-
sulted constant the type is always read, and the value is read only for definitions. The value
of a theorem, once reached, is not read.


Lemma 12.15 (Interface lemma). Assume Convention 12.12. Let T be a theorem of Γ with type
φ and value v, and let Γ′ be obtained by replacing v with a term v′ such that T  : φ := v′ checks in
the prefix of Γ before T. Then every constant c̸ = T that checks in Γ also checks in Γ′.


Proof. Here “c checks in Γ” means that the typing derivation of the declaration c is valid
relative to the constants preceding it. A constant before T is unchanged and cannot men-
tion T. For a constant c after T, a derivation of c in Γ uses, for each occurrence of T, only
the type φ by (K1) and (K2), since T is a theorem and is never unfolded; and for any other
constant e it uses data identical in Γ and Γ′ (types always, and values of definitions, which
are unchanged). The same derivation is therefore a derivation in Γ′.           ■


Theorem 12.16 (Typed blast radius). Assume Convention 12.12. Let Γ′ be obtained from Γ by
replacing the value of the constant D by one that checks at D’s type. Let c̸ = D be a constant after
D that checks in Γ.
  (a)  If D is a theorem then c checks in Γ′.
 (b)  If D is a definition and D /∈Cons(c) then c checks in Γ′.
  (c)  If D is a definition and D ∈Cons(c), then c need not check in Γ′.


Proof. (a) is Lemma 12.15. (b) By Definition 12.14 and (K1), the derivation of c reads the
value only of definitions in Cons(c) and the type of constants in Cons(c), and c’s own data;
D is not among them, so the derivation transfers unchanged. (c) Let D  : N := 0 and
c : D = 0 := rfl, checks since D unfolds to 0. Replace the value of D by 1. Then c no longer
type-checks, since 1̸ ≡0.                                    ■


  Theorem 12.16 gives a prediction rule for mutations of a verified development: replac-
ing the value of a theorem breaks nothing, replacing the value of a definition can break
only constants for which the definition is consulted, and in the flat graph the second set
is overestimated by paths through theorem bodies and the first is overestimated entirely.
A prediction made with the flat graph that treats a path through a theorem body as a
dependency will predict breakage that does not occur; a prediction that treats an edge
to a definition in a type as opaque will miss breakage that does. Chapter 18 records the
preregistered mutation matrix in which two mutants, M09 and M16, had outcomes that
contradicted the prediction of the flat model; the typed edges above are the amendment,
and the two mutants are retained there as falsified under the earlier model, not corrected
after the fact.

Part IV

Admissibility of Search

Chapter 13

Search States as Worlds




Part III asked what a finished result retains. Part IV asks the corresponding question of
the process that produces results, at the level of individual steps. A search procedure re-
peatedly selects an item, derives new items from it, discards items it judges unnecessary,
and sometimes replaces its whole state by a smaller one. Each of these is an operation on
a state, and the correctness of a prover lives in which of the operations preserve which
of the state’s distinctions. This chapter gives the operations names and the state a pre-
cise structure, and proves four things: the option space of a search is changed only by
refusal (Proposition 13.5); a refusal is lossless exactly when the refused item is redundant
(Proposition 13.5(c)); the extensional state is the minimal representation that supports ev-
ery future of the search (Theorem 13.8); and proofs are not recoverable from that state
(Proposition 13.11).
  The vocabulary of four operations, pop, refuse, bind and collapse, follows the author’s
earlier work on binding and on disposition calculi [35, 36]. Nothing from those works is
assumed. Every definition is restated for search, and every result below is proved from the
definitions given here.


13.1  Closure systems and option spaces

Fix a set F of items, for instance clauses, and an inference system I over F in the sense of
Definition 2.1.

Definition 13.1 (Option closure). A closure operator on 2F is a map Cn that is extensive
(S ⊆Cn(S)), monotone (S ⊆S′ implies Cn(S) ⊆Cn(S′)) and idempotent (Cn(Cn(S)) =
Cn(S)).  It respects I if Cn(S) is saturated for every S: whenever (Q, c) is a rule instance
with Q ⊆Cn(S) then c ∈Cn(S).

Example 13.2 (Derivation closure). Let CnI(S) be the set of items having a derivation tree
from S: leaves in S, internal nodes instances of rules of I. It is extensive (a one-node tree),
monotone, and idempotent (a tree over leaves from CnI(S) is grafted onto trees from S).
It respects I by the same grafting. For resolution, Chapter 3 writes this as the set of clauses
derivable from S.

  The closure is the option closure: Cn(S) is everything still obtainable from the premises
S. A second closure, adapted to redundancy, is introduced in Chapter 14.

13.2. WORLDS                                                               81

13.2  Worlds

Definition 13.3 (Events, histories, state). Fix an initial set S0 ⊆F. An event is one of
   • Pop(f): select the item f for processing;
   • Refuse(f): declare f inadmissible as a premise from now on;
   • Bind(r; f1, . . . , fn ⊢f): derive f from f1, . . . , fn by a rule instance r = ({f1, . . . , fn}, f) ∈
     R.
A history is a finite sequence of events. To each history H attach a triple ρ(H) = (D, R, P)
of sets of items, the extensional state, by recursion: ρ(ε) = (S0, ∅, ∅) and, writing ρ(H) =
(D, R, P),
   • Pop(f) is well formed iff f ∈D \ (R ∪P), and ρ(H · Pop(f)) = (D, R, P ∪{f});
   • Refuse(f) is well formed iff f ∈D \ R, and ρ(H · Refuse(f)) = (D, R ∪{f}, P);
   • Bind(r;⃗f ⊢f) is well formed iff⃗f ⊆P \ R and f /∈D, and ρ(H · Bind(r;⃗f ⊢f)) =
    (D ∪{f}, R, P).

A history is well formed if every event is well formed at its point. Write D(H), R(H), P(H)
for the components; D is the set of derived items, R the refused, P the popped. The available
items are Av(H) = D(H)\R(H), the option space is Ω(H) = Cn(Av(H)), and the provenance
π(H) is the set of Bind events occurring in H. A world is a well-formed history regarded
together with its option space.

  A world is the pair that the framework calls (history, option space). The history is
append-only: nothing is removed from D or R, and the option space is a derived quantity
that can shrink. Two features of the definition matter below. A refused item is never un-
refused. And a Bind derives only items not already derived, so D is a set and an item has
exactly one recorded justification, the first.

Example 13.4 (The given-clause loop as a history). In the given-clause algorithm of Sec-
tion 2.2, one iteration selects a clause g from the unprocessed pool (Pop(g)), derives con-
clusions between g and the processed clauses (a sequence of Bind events), and removes
clauses found redundant (Refuse events). The sequence of all events of a run is a well-
formed history whose extensional state at each point is the triple (all clauses ever gener-
ated, all clauses discarded, all clauses selected). The loop of Chapter 2 is thus a particular
strategy for extending histories, and the transition system of Definition 2.6 is the transition
system of worlds restricted to that strategy.


13.3  The option space moves only under refusal

Proposition 13.5 (Dynamics of the option space). Let Cn be a closure operator respecting I,
and let H be well formed.
  (a) Ω(H · Pop(f)) = Ω(H) whenever the event is well formed.
  (b) Ω(H · Bind(r;⃗f ⊢f)) = Ω(H) whenever the event is well formed.
  (c) Ω(H · Refuse(f)) ⊆Ω(H) whenever the event is well formed, with equality if and only if
     f ∈Cn(Av(H) \ {f}).

Proof. Write A = Av(H). (a) Pop changes only P, so A is unchanged. (b) The premises⃗
f lie in A, hence in Cn(A) by extensivity, and Cn(A) is saturated, so f ∈Cn(A). The new

set of available items is A ∪{f} ⊆Cn(A). By monotonicity and idempotence Cn(A) ⊆
Cn(A ∪{f}) ⊆Cn(Cn(A)) = Cn(A).
   (c) The new available set is A \ {f} (here f ∈A by well-formedness), so containment
follows from monotonicity. If f ∈Cn(A \ {f}) then A ⊆Cn(A \ {f}) by extensivity, so
Cn(A) ⊆Cn(Cn(A\{f})) = Cn(A\{f}), which is equality. Conversely if the two closures
coincide then f ∈A ⊆Cn(A) = Cn(A \ {f}).                        ■

Corollary 13.6 (Search is movement within a fixed space). For every well-formed H, Ω(H) ⊆
Ω(ε) = Cn(S0), and Ω(H) = Cn(S0) if H contains no Refuse event. In particular, in a refusal-free
history every item that will ever be derived already lies in the option space at the start, and progress
consists of making items derived (members of D), not of enlarging what is obtainable.


Proof. Induct on the length of H using Proposition 13.5. The base case is the definition,
since Av(ε) = S0.                                        ■


  The corollary has a practical meaning that is seldom stated. Every time a prover discards
an item, it makes a bet about the option space, because discarding is the only operation
that can change it; and conversely every eﬀiciency gain from deletion is paid for by the
possibility that the bet is wrong. Proposition 13.5(c) says exactly when it is not.

Definition 13.7 (Lossless refusal). A well-formed event Refuse(f) at H is lossless if Ω(H ·
Refuse(f)) = Ω(H), and lossless for a goal g ∈F if g ∈Ω(H) implies g ∈Ω(H · Refuse(f)).

   Proposition 13.5(c) characterizes lossless refusal: the refused item must already be obtain-
able from the other available items. This is the semantic notion of redundancy that the next
chapter specialises. A refusal that is lossy for some goals may still be admissible if the goals
are not asked for, which is the task-relative notion of Chapter 10 and is the content of the
next section.


13.4  The extensional state is the minimal state for all futures

Theorem 13.8 (Future equivalence). Let H, H′ be well-formed histories with ρ(H) = ρ(H′).
Then for every event e, e is well formed after H if and only if it is after H′, and ρ(H ·e) = ρ(H′ ·e).
Consequently, with Ffut = {H 7→ρ(H · w)  : w an event sequence} (defined where H · w is
well formed, and by a fixed symbol ∗elsewhere), one has ker Ffut = ker ρ, so ρ is the minimal
Ffut-suﬀicient representation of well-formed histories (Theorem 10.4).

Proof. Well-formedness and the state update in Definition 13.3 refer only to the current
triple and the event. Hence equal triples treat every event identically, and induction on the
length of w gives equal behaviour on all continuations. For the kernel: taking w = ε shows
ker Ffut ⊆ker ρ, and the first part shows ker ρ ⊆ker Ffut.                  ■

  The option space is a function of the extensional state, Ω= Cn(D \ R), so any repre-
sentation suﬀicient for all futures determines it. The theorem has a converse in spirit: a
collapse of worlds that identifies two histories with different extensional states changes
the set of continuations that are well formed or the states they lead to, so the collapse is
not a congruence for the dynamics. The exact formulation follows.

13.5. PROVENANCE IS NOT IN THE STATE                                     83


Definition 13.9 (Collapse, two conditions). A collapse is a representation σ : W →Q on the
set W of well-formed histories. Let F be a task family on W. σ is F-suﬀicient if it satisfies
the condition of Definition 10.2 for F. σ is refusal-respecting if ker σ ⊆ker Av, that is, if
σ(H) = σ(H′) implies Av(H) = Av(H′). It is admissible for F if it is both.

  By Theorem 10.4, admissibility for F is suﬀiciency for F ∪{Av}, and by Theorem 10.7
it is automatic exactly when Av is computable from F. The two conditions are in general
independent, and each is violated by natural collapses.

Proposition 13.10 (Independence of the two conditions). There are a task prov and collapses
σ1, σ2 of well-formed histories such that σ1 is {prov}-suﬀicient but not refusal-respecting, and σ2
is refusal-respecting but not {prov}-suﬀicient. Moreover there is a collapse that is suﬀicient for the
verdict task unsat(H) = [⊥∈Ω(H)] but not for continuation.

Proof. Take the task prov(H) = π(H). Let σ1 = π; it is {prov}-suﬀicient trivially. It is not
refusal-respecting: for S0 = {a, b} with no rules, the histories ε and Refuse(a) have the same
provenance ∅and different available sets. Let σ2 = Av, trivially refusal-respecting. It is not
{prov}-suﬀicient: with S0 = {p, q, r} and rules r1 = ({p, q}, c), r2 = ({p, r}, c), the histories
H1 = Pop(p), Pop(q), Bind(r1; p, q ⊢c) and H2 = Pop(p), Pop(r), Bind(r2; p, r ⊢c) have
Av = {p, q, r, c} in both and different provenance. For the last statement take σ3 = unsat
and S0 = {a, b} without rules. Neither ε nor Refuse(a) derives ⊥, so σ3 identifies them, yet
Pop(a) is well formed after the first and not after the second.               ■

  The proof is deliberately elementary. The significance lies in the pattern it exhibits: a
representation that is exactly suﬀicient for the question being asked now (the verdict, the
proof, the count) is generally insuﬀicient for continuation, and continuation is what a search
is. The standing recommendation of the chapter is therefore the following.

 A collapse in search is admissible only relative to a declared task and a declared
  continuation. Preserve F for the present question (Chapter 10); preserve Av if later
  events are to behave as they would have; preserve the full extensional state ρ if the
  search is to be resumed exactly (Theorem 13.8); and preserve provenance π if proofs
  are to be extracted (Proposition 13.11).


13.5  Provenance is not in the state


Proposition 13.11 (Proofs are not a function of the extensional state). There are well-formed
histories H1, H2 with ρ(H1) = ρ(H2) and π(H1)̸ = π(H2) in which the two recorded justifications
of the item c yield derivation trees of c with different sets of leaves. Hence the task “return a derivation
of c from S0” is not ρ-suﬀicient, and by Theorem 13.8 the extensional state, which suﬀices for all
future behaviour of the search, does not suﬀice for extracting a proof.

Proof. The histories of the preceding proof have equal ρ = ({p, q, r, c}, ∅, {p, q, r}) only if
both pop all of p, q, r; extend H1 by Pop(r) and H2 by Pop(q). Then ρ(H1) = ρ(H2), while
the derivation of c read from π has leaves {p, q} in H1 and {p, r} in H2.          ■

   This is the world-level counterpart of the residue of Chapter 1: the proof extracted from
a run is a function of π, the extensional state is a function of the run, and neither determines

Definition 13.12 (Attainable outcomes). A continuation of a well-formed H is an event

Chapter 15 makes this precise for finite clause universes; in general it means that no Pop or
Bind is well formed). The outcome of a terminal H · w is refuted if ⊥∈D \ R and saturated
otherwise. The set of attainable outcomes of H is

              C(H) = {out(H · w) : w a terminal continuation of H}.

  A collapse or refusal q is then judged against a declared outcome task. For refutation the
condition is refuted ∈C(H) ⇐⇒refuted ∈C(q(H)), which Chapter 14 establishes for the
admissible refusals. For repair and diagnosis the condition is too weak: it says that a cer-
tificate remains obtainable, not that the distinctions needed to explain or adjust the search
remain recorded, and those are the tasks of Chapter 11. The two kinds of requirement
correspond to two different representations, the first through Ωand the second through
(ρ, π).

  Two properties of an execution are easily conflated and are logically independent. De-
fine a raw history to be a sequence of events with no well-formedness requirement, with the
state updates of Definition 13.3 applied unconditionally.

Definition 13.13 (Logical soundness and refusal-respect). A raw history is logically sound
if every item added to D by a Bind event is entailed by the items it was derived from (for
an inference system with a semantics, as in Definition 2.1). It is refusal-respecting if no event
uses, as a premise of a Bind or as the target of a Pop, an item that is in R at that time.

Proposition 13.14 (Independence). There are raw histories that are logically sound but not
refusal-respecting, and raw histories that are refusal-respecting but not logically sound. A well-
formed history over a sound inference system is both.

Proof. Let S0 =  {p, p →q} with →-elimination as the only rule.  The raw history
Pop(p), Pop(p →q), Refuse(p), Bind(→E; p, p →q ⊢q) derives only valid consequences
and uses the refused p as a premise.  For the converse let the rule set contain the un-
sound instance ({p}, q) with S0 = {p}; Pop(p), Bind({p} ⊢q) respects every refusal and
adds q, which is not entailed.  For the last statement, well-formedness is the refusal-
respecting condition by definition, and logical soundness follows from soundness of the
rule instances.                                          ■

   Logical soundness is a property of the rule set, assured by a checker for the rules.
Refusal-respect is a property of the execution, assured by the gate of Chapter 15. A proof
produced by a run that used a refused premise is a valid proof and a violation of the
run’s recorded restrictions; a run that respects every refusal and applies an unsound rule
violates nothing recorded and proves nothing. The lifecycle of Chapter 16 separates the
same two things by assigning the first to verifiers and the second to disposition authority.
