Chapter 14

Redundancy as Admissible Collapse




Provers discard clauses. Without deletion, saturation procedures drown in consequences
that add nothing, and every serious implementation removes tautologies and subsumed
clauses as a matter of course.  In the vocabulary of Chapter 13, deletion is Refuse, and
Proposition 13.5 says that it is the only event that changes the option space. This chapter
proves that for propositional resolution the two standard deletions are admissible, in the
strongest sense that fair runs with deletion remain refutationally complete, and shows by
a small example that the admissibility of a refusal is a property of the current world and
not of the refused item alone.

  Throughout, clauses are finite sets of literals as in Chapter 3, Res(S) denotes the set of
clauses derivable from S by resolution (including S itself), and I is propositional resolu-
tion.


14.1 A closure adapted to redundancy

The closure Res is the wrong option closure for deletion. If D ⊊C and C is refused while
D remains available, then C ∈Av is typically not in Res(Av \ {C}), because resolution
never weakens a clause. So by Proposition 13.5(c) the refusal is lossy for Res, although
every use that could be made of C can be made of D (Exercise in Chapter 13). The remedy
is to measure options up to redundancy.

Definition 14.1 (Redundancy closure). For a set N of clauses let

            ↑∗N = {C : C is a tautology, or E ⊆C for some E ∈N},

and put Cn⊑(S) = ↑∗Res(S).

  A clause is in Cn⊑(S) if it is derivable up to subsumption, or is a tautology (which is
entailed by everything).

Lemma 14.2 (Lifting through redundancy). Let N be a set of clauses that is saturated up to
redundancy: every resolvent of two members of N lies in ↑∗N. Then every clause derivable by
resolution from ↑∗N lies in ↑∗N.

Proof. Induct on the derivation. Premises from ↑∗N are trivially in it. Let C = C′1 ∪C′2 be
the resolvent on l of C1 = C′1 ∪{l} and C2 = C′2 ∪{l}, both in ↑∗N.

l /∈E1 then E1 ⊆C′1 ⊆C, so C ∈↑∗N; likewise if l /∈E2. Otherwise E1 = E′1 ∪{l} and

14.2  Tautology and subsumption refusal

Theorem 14.4 (Admissible refusals). Let H be a well-formed history, f ∈Av(H) and A =
Av(H). Refusing f is lossless for Ω= Cn⊑(Av) in each of the cases
  (i) f is a tautology;
  (ii) f is subsumed: there is D ∈A \ {f} with D ⊆f.
In particular, in both cases unsat(H · Refuse(f)) = unsat(H).

Proof. By Proposition 13.5(c) it suﬀices to show f ∈Cn⊑(A \ {f}). In case (i), f ∈↑∗(·)
by definition. In case (ii), D ∈A \ {f} ⊆Res(A \ {f}) and D ⊆f, so f ∈↑∗Res(A \ {f}).
Proposition 14.3 supplies the closure properties used by Proposition 13.5, and the last claim
follows since □∈Ωis the verdict.                               ■

  The theorem is the formal sense of the slogan that redundancy is lossless refusal. Note
that the witness D must lie in the current available set. This is exactly where history enters.

Example 14.5 (Duplicates and the witness that was already refused). Let items be occur-
rences of clauses, so that two occurrences c1, c2 may carry the same clause {a}, and let
S0 = {c1, c2, c3} with c3 = {¬a}. The set is unsatisfiable. The refusal Refuse(c1) is admis-
sible, since the available c2 carries the same clause. After it, Refuse(c2) is not lossless: the
available set is {c3}, which is satisfiable. A refusal criterion that accepts a witness among
all items seen so far, available or refused, would approve both steps and destroy the refu-
tation. The criterion of Theorem 14.4 is correct because it quantifies over Av(H), not over
D(H).

14.3  Completeness with deletion

The fairness theorem of Chapter 2 (Theorem 2.4) is stated for increasing chains N0 ⊆N1 ⊆
· · · and does not apply to a procedure that deletes.  It must be replaced by an argument
about persistent clauses and the witnesses that justify each deletion. Lossless refusals pre-
serve refutability at each step. A prover must also find the refutation, and an infinite se-
quence of individually admissible refusals could in principle remove every witness in turn.
The following theorem shows that for propositional resolution under a fair strategy, it can-
not.

Chapter 15

Guidance and the Verifier Gate




The search procedures of Part I choose their next step by fixed rules: oldest clause first,
smallest clause first, a weighted mixture. Modern systems replace the rule by a learned
model that proposes the next step, a premise to use, a tactic to try, a lemma to add. This
chapter asks what such a proposer can change and what it cannot. The answer has two
halves. In the world model of Chapter 13, a proposal is an event, and only Refuse and
collapse change the option space, so guidance that merely orders Pop and Bind events can-
not affect what is obtainable (Section 15.1). Guidance that proposes refusals can, and the
second half separates proposals from acceptance: a gate that checks each proposed event
against a decidable criterion makes the proposer irrelevant for soundness and for complete-
ness, and an ungated proposer is shown to be capable of destroying both (Sections 15.2
and 15.3). The last section proves in abstract form that a gate which can see only what
the proposer sees cannot discriminate between situations the proposer cannot distinguish
(Section 15.4).


15.1  Ordering does not change the option space


Retain the setting of Chapter 14: propositional resolution over a finite set S0, worlds with
Ω= Cn⊑(Av), and refusals restricted to the admissible forms of Theorem 14.4.

Lemma 15.1 (Runs are finite and maximal runs are fair). Every well-formed history over a
finite clause universe has length at most 3N, where N is the number of clauses over the atoms of S0.
Call a history saturating if no Pop or Bind event is well formed after it. Every history extends to a
saturating one, and every saturating history is a fair run in the sense of Definition 14.6.


Proof. Each Pop adds an item to P, each Refuse adds an item to R, each Bind adds an item
to D, and these sets only grow within a set of size N; the bound follows. Extension to a
saturating history is by repeatedly adding well-formed Pop and Bind events, which termi-
nates by the bound. For fairness, let a resolution instance have both premises persistent,
that is, available at the end.  If its conclusion E were not in D at the end, then Pop of
any unpopped available premise would be well formed, contradicting saturation, so both
premises are popped and available, and Bind of the instance is well formed, contradicting
saturation again. Hence E ∈D.                                ■

Theorem 15.2 (Guidance is irrelevant to completeness). Let S0 be a finite unsatisfiable set of
clauses and let H be any saturating history all of whose Refuse events are admissible in the sense
of Theorem 14.4. Then □∈D(H) \ R(H), whatever the order of the Pop and Bind events. In
particular this holds for histories produced by any selection function, learned or otherwise, provided
it does not stop before saturation.

Proof. By Lemma 15.1 the history is a fair run with admissible deletion. Apply Theo-
rem 14.7.                                             ■

  The theorem is not a statement that guidance is useless. The length of the history, the
number of items derived before □appears, and the memory used all depend strongly on
the order. What it excludes is a different claim, sometimes made implicitly: that a better
selection function can change which refutations exist. In the language of Chapter 13, selec-
tion acts within a fixed space (Corollary 13.6). A formal reading of “the model found a
proof the baseline could not find” is therefore always a statement about a resource bound,
never about the option space, unless the model’s proposals include refusals or collapses.

Remark 15.3 (Early stopping). The hypothesis “does not stop before saturation” cannot
be dropped. A guided procedure that stops at a time limit is not a saturating run, and
Theorem 15.2 says nothing about it. Its power is the probability, over inputs, that □has
appeared by the time limit, which is a property of the guidance and the distribution of
inputs. No such probability is computed in this book.


15.2  The verifier gate

Definition 15.4 (Proposer, gate, gated run). A proposer is an arbitrary function Prop from
histories to events. It need not be computable, deterministic, or sound; a language model
with sampling is an example, understood as a nondeterministic proposer. The gate for
refutation of clause sets is the decidable predicate Gate(H, e) that holds iff e is well formed
after H and, in case e = Refuse(f), f is a tautology or is subsumed by some D ∈Av(H)\{f}.
A gated run starting from ε applies the proposed event if the gate accepts it and discards it
otherwise.

Theorem 15.5 (Gate separates the proposer from soundness and completeness). Let S0 be
a finite set of clauses.

  (i) Soundness. For every proposer, every gated run is a well-formed history with admissible
       refusals, every f ∈D(H) is a consequence of S0, and □∈D(H) implies S0 is unsatisfiable.
  (ii) Completeness.  If S0 is unsatisfiable and the proposer is exhaustive, in the sense that at
      every history at which some Pop or Bind event is well formed it eventually proposes one, then
      every gated run extends to □∈D(H) \ R(H).
 (iii) Necessity of exhaustiveness. There are finite unsatisfiable S0 and non-exhaustive proposers
     whose gated runs never derive □.

Proof. (i) Every applied event satisfies the gate, so is well formed and, if a refusal, admissi-
ble. Every f ∈D(H) is in S0 or is the conclusion of a sound rule instance with premises in
D(H), so is a consequence of S0 by induction (Proposition 3.2). If □∈D(H) then S0 |= □.
   (ii) A gated run with an exhaustive proposer continues until no Pop or Bind is well
formed, that is, to a saturating history, since the run is finite by Lemma 15.1 and each stage

15.3. UNGATED PROPOSALS                                                  93


at which an event is well formed will eventually see one proposed and, if well formed,
accepted. Apply Theorem 15.2.
    (iii) Let S0 = {{a}, {¬a}} and let the proposer propose only Refuse events that the gate
rejects. The run is ε forever; □/∈D(ε).                            ■


  The architectural content of the theorem is Theorem 1.5 of Chapter 1 in the setting of
search: assurance attaches to the gate, and the producer may be arbitrarily unreliable with-
out affecting soundness. Completeness is an exhaustiveness property of the producer, and
exhaustiveness is cheap to impose: any proposer can be wrapped to fall back to a fixed fair
strategy every kth step, at a cost of at most a factor k in the length of the history.

15.4  Self-contained gates cannot discriminate what the proposer
     cannot


The gate of Definition 15.4 is decidable and external: it reads the history and the clause,
which are the same objects the checker of Chapter 1 reads. A different design asks the
proposer, or another model sharing its inputs, to judge its own outputs. The structural
limit of such a design is a consequence of Proposition 1.12, and is stated here in the abstract
form it will be needed in (see also [38]).

Definition 15.7 (Environments, evidence, gate). Let E be a set of environments (the situa-
tions in which a proposal will be used), Z a set of evidence states, and z : E →Z the evidence
map. A correct action is a function α : E →{accept, reject}. A gate restricted to z is a function
G ◦z with G : Z →{accept, reject}. It is correct if G ◦z = α.


Theorem 15.8 (Impossibility of self-contained gates). A correct gate restricted to z exists if
and only if α is constant on every fibre of z. In particular, if e0, e1 ∈E satisfy z(e0) = z(e1) and
α(e0)̸ = α(e1), then no gate restricted to z is correct, however it is constructed and however much
computation it uses.


Proof. This is Proposition 1.12 for the task α and the representation z. For the second state-
ment, a gate G ◦z takes the same value at e0 and e1.                    ■


Corollary 15.9 (A signal from outside the evidence class is necessary). Let α be a correct-
action function not constant on some fibre of z. Any correct gate must read a quantity not determined
by z. Adding to the gate a function of z, such as the proposer’s own confidence or an independent
run of a model that sees the same inputs, leaves the set of indistinguishable pairs unchanged.


Proof. A gate reading z and a function u(z) is a function of z; Theorem 15.8 applies.   ■


   In proof search, an example is immediate. Let an environment consist of a statement φ
together with its status (provable or not), and let the evidence be a natural-language justifi-
cation produced by a model. If the model produces the same justification for a provable φ0
and an unprovable φ1 (as a fluent but wrong argument might), then by Theorem 15.8 no
judge that sees only the justification can accept one and reject the other. The kernel check
Chk(d, φ) is not subject to the theorem because its evidence is (d, φ) together with the inde-
pendently defined meaning of Chk, a function of the environment that is not determined
by what the model emitted. This is the content of the independence principle of Chapter 1
in the abstract setting.

Chapter 16

Lifecycle and Authority




A search step changes a world. A claim, however, has a life that extends beyond a single
search: it is opened as a goal, tied to evidence and obligations, transformed as it is repaired
or reformulated, verified, and eventually accepted or rejected. This chapter models that
life as a small labelled transition system, proves two safety properties of it, and shows that
the most natural-looking simplification, treating a failed verification as a refusal, destroys
exactly the repairability that Chapter 11 showed to be essential. The first property is about
what must have happened before a claim is collapsed into an accepted state. The second is
about who may do it: verifiers report results and never gain the authority to dispose of a
claim.


16.1  The machine

Definition 16.1 (Lifecycle machine). Fix a finite set Obl of obligations, for instance the layers
O1 to O3 of Chapter 9 together with any declared by the claim. A configuration is a triple
(q, v, W) where
   • q ∈{open, bound, transformed, verified, verificationFailed, refused, collapsed} is the sta-
       tus;
   • v ∈N is the artifact version;
   • W ⊆Obl is the set of obligations verified at version v.
The initial configuration is (open, 0, ∅). Each transition is labelled by an event and an actor,
either disp (a disposition authority) or ver (a verifier):

                                fused, collapsed

16.2. COLLAPSE SAFETY                                                      97


The statuses refused and collapsed are terminal: no transition leaves them. The statuses other
than the terminal ones are live.

  The table adopts three design decisions. (1) Every Transform clears W: a verification
is a statement about one version of the artifact and does not survive its replacement. (2)
Refuse is permitted from every live status, so the disposition authority can always decline
to continue, which corresponds to the append-only refusal set of Chapter 13. (3) verifica-
tionFailed is a live status: its outgoing transitions are Transform and Refuse.
  The open status has no verify transition: a claim must first be bound to the obligations
it will be verified against.


16.2  Collapse safety


Theorem 16.2 (Collapse requires current, complete verification). In every reachable configu-
ration with q = collapsed one has W = Obl. Moreover in every trace reaching such a configuration,
for each o ∈Obl the last event concerning o among {VerifyOK(o), VerifyFail(o)} is a VerifyOK(o),
and no Transform occurs after the first of these final VerifyOK events.

Proof. Invariant. Every reachable configuration with q = verified has W = Obl. This holds
because verified is entered only by VerifyOK when the new W equals Obl, and the only
transitions that change W from a status verified are Transform, which leaves verified. The
status collapsed is entered only by Collapse from verified, with W unchanged, so W = Obl.
   Trace claim. Let the trace end in collapsed. Let t be the last Transform in the trace, or the
start if none. After t, W = ∅at the moment t occurs, and W grows only by VerifyOK events.
Since W = Obl at collapse, every o has a VerifyOK(o) after t. Between that event and the
collapse there is no VerifyFail(o): a VerifyFail moves to verificationFailed, from which the only
exits are Transform and Refuse, and there is no Transform after t, while Refuse is terminal.
So the last event concerning o is a VerifyOK(o), and it comes after the last Transform.  ■

  The theorem is the lifecycle form of a requirement stated in Chapter 12: an inherited veri-
fication is a fact about a particular version. A claim that has been verified, then transformed,
and then collapsed without re-verification is excluded by the machine and not merely dis-
couraged. It also interacts with Chapter 9: since Obl includes the layers beyond O1, the ma-
chine can enter verified only after an actor outside the kernel has produced VerifyOK(O2)
and VerifyOK(O3). The kernel is one verifier among several, and it can contribute only
VerifyOK(O1).


16.3  Authority is not verification

Theorem 16.3 (Verifiers do not dispose). Every transition whose actor is ver has target sta-
tus in {bound, transformed, verified, verificationFailed}, and none has target refused or collapsed.
Consequently no sequence of verifier events alone reaches a terminal status, and the set of terminal
statuses reachable from a configuration depends on verifier events only through which disposition
events become enabled.

Proof. Inspection of the table: the verifier events VerifyOK and VerifyFail have the stated
targets, and the only events with targets refused, collapsed are Refuse and Collapse, both

with actor disp. A sequence of verifier events cannot contain an event leaving a live status
through a disposition label, so it stays live. The last sentence restates that Collapse is enabled
exactly at verified, a status that verifier events can produce.                 ■

  The separation is the lifecycle counterpart of the gate of Chapter 15. The gate rejects pro-
posals; it does not decide what to propose. Here the verifier reports; it does not decide the
fate of the claim. A system in which a verifier’s negative report removes a claim from cir-
culation has assigned the verifier a disposition authority that the verifier’s own assurance
does not warrant, since a failed check is not a refutation (Chapter 1).


16.4 Why a failed verification must stay live

Consider the variant machine L′ in which the target of every VerifyFail(o) transition is re-
fused instead of verificationFailed.

Proposition 16.4 (Automatic refusal destroys repair). In the machine of Definition 16.1 there
is a trace reaching collapsed that contains a VerifyFail event. In L′ no trace containing a VerifyFail
event reaches collapsed.

Proof. Take Obl = {O1}. The trace Bind, VerifyFail(O1), Transform, VerifyOK(O1), Collapse
is valid: after the failure the status is verificationFailed, whose exits include Transform (to
transformed at version 1 with W = ∅); VerifyOK(O1) gives W = Obl and status verified, and
Collapse follows. In L′ the same VerifyFail moves to refused, which is terminal.      ■

   Proposition 16.4 is the lifecycle form of Chapter 11. The repair of a failed result, the
replacement of an artifact by a nearby one, is a transition out of verificationFailed.  If the
failure refuses, there is nothing to repair, and the option space of the claim, in the sense of
Chapter 13, has been reduced by an actor who was not authorized to reduce it. Formally:
the set of terminal statuses reachable from verificationFailed is {refused, collapsed} in L and
{refused} in L′.

Remark 16.5 (Information in a failure). The statement of Theorem 11.13 applies to the fail-
ure itself: what is retained in verificationFailed should include which obligation failed, on
which version, and with which witness, because the repair relation of Definition 11.12
reads that information. The machine records only the status; the history carries the rest.


16.5  Reachability and history


The machine is deliberately small enough to be explored exhaustively. With a bound on the
version, the configuration space is finite, and the claims above were checked by exhaustive
enumeration of all traces up to a fixed length for |Obl| = 2 and 3 (no violations). The proofs
given are the general ones; enumeration is a check on the table.

Proposition 16.6 (Histories are not recoverable from configurations). A live configuration
always has an enabled event, so every maximal finite trace ends in a terminal status. Two distinct
traces can end in the same configuration, so the final configuration does not determine the history.

Proof. Refuse is enabled at every live status. The traces Refuse and Bind, Refuse both end in
(refused, 0, ∅) and differ. This is the analogue of Proposition 13.11 for lifecycles.     ■

16.6. PROPOSED EXTENSION: TYPED MEMORY CONSOLIDATION              99

16.6  Proposed extension: typed memory consolidation


This section is a proposed formalization.  It does not describe the guarantees of any implemented
memory system, and no property of the retrieval dynamics of such a system is assumed.

  The lifecycle machine governs one claim. A system that stores many claims and the
traces that produced them has the further problem of consolidation: replacing the full his-
tory by a smaller memory representation. The elements of the preceding chapters combine
into a small calculus for this, in which retrieval guides search, verification is separate from
commitment, and consolidation is an admissible collapse.

Definition 16.7 (Memory configuration). A memory configuration is S = (H, M, K, ν)
where H is an append-only event history, M a memory representation, K a finite set
of commit capabilities, and ν ∈N the environment version, which counts the changes to
assumptions, policy or checking environment. Items are triples m = (p, η, ϱ): payload,
retrieval parameters, provenance reference. Events are Recall(q, L), Verify(m, v), Permit(m),
Commit(m, k), Refuse(m, r), Reopen(m, r), Env(δ), Transport(m, w) and Consolidate(c). Fix
a family F of future tasks on histories.

  Evidence is indexed by version. Define by recursion on H the sets Ver(H) and Perm(H)
of items currently verified and currently permitted: both start empty; Verify(m, v) adds m to
Ver and Permit(m) adds m to Perm; Env(δ) empties both and increments ν; Transport(m, w),
applicable immediately after an Env and only when w witnesses that the obligations behind
the verification (respectively permission) of m survive that change, restores m to the set in
which it stood before the Env; Refuse(m, ·) removes m from both sets. The witness w plays
the role of the interface lemma of Chapter 12: it is a certificate that the consulted set of the
verification is disjoint from what the change touched.

  The transition rules are:
   • Recall(q, L) may be applied to any configuration; it appends the event and returns a
        list L of candidates. Candidates carry no standing: recall changes neither verification,
     permission, nor commitment status.
   • Verify(m, v) is applied when v is a witness of the declared verification condition
    VH(m) for the current history and version; it appends the event.
   • Permit(m) is applied by the disposition authority when policy at the current version
     permits commitment of m.
   • Commit(m, k) is applicable only if m ∈Ver(H) ∩Perm(H) and k ∈K; it removes k
     from K and appends the event.
   • Refuse(m, r) appends the event. Reopen(m, r) is applicable only to a refused item, by
     the disposition authority, and appends the event with its reason. A reopened item
     has no current evidence until it is verified and permitted again.
   • Env(δ) and Transport(m, w) act on versions as just described.
   • Consolidate(c) replaces M by the pair (c(H), ε) and is applicable only if c : H →M
       is F-extension-suﬀicient: c(H1) = c(H2) implies f(H1H′′) = f(H2H′′) for every f ∈F
     and every suﬀix H′′. Subsequent events are appended to the second component of
    M.

Definition 16.8 (Invariants). A configuration is well founded if (I1) every committed m
was in Ver ∩Perm of the prefix of H immediately before its Commit, that is, had evidence
for the version current at commitment; (I2) the capabilities used by the Commit events in

H are pairwise distinct and disjoint from K; (I3) every Reopen(m, r) in H is preceded by
a Refuse(m, ·); (I4) M = (c(H′), H′′) for a factorization H = H′H′′ and an F-extension-
suﬀicient c whose consolidation event ends H′, or M is the initial representation.

Theorem 16.9 (Preservation of memory invariants).  If S is well founded and S →S′ by any
rule above, then S′ is well founded. Moreover recall never changes the set of committed items.

Proof. By cases on the rule. I1 concerns the prefix before each Commit and so is untouched
by any rule except a new Commit, which satisfies it by applicability. Commit(m, k) removes
k from K while recording it in H, so the used capabilities remain pairwise distinct (since

other rules leave K and the used set unchanged. Reopen is applicable only after a refusal,
which gives I3; the other rules do not add a Reopen. For I4, every rule other than Consolidate
appends an event to H and to the second component of M, preserving the factorization;
Consolidate(c) is applicable only for extension-suﬀicient c and sets H′ = H, H′′ = ε. For
the last statement, only Commit changes the set of committed items.           ■

a commitment forces either a fresh verification or a transport witness. The cost of the latter

Proposition 16.10 (Memory answers current-history tasks).  If M = (c(H′), H′′) with c
extension-suﬀicient, then for each f ∈F the value f(H′H′′) is a function of M alone.

determines ¯g and its argument.                                ■

Nerode: the coarsest suﬀicient encoder is the quotient of histories by the relation H1 ∼H2
iff f(H1H′′) = f(H2H′′) for all f ∈F and all H′′, and by Theorem 10.4 the suﬀicient

for tasks on the history at the moment of consolidation is not enough once new events
arrive, which is why the weaker condition ker c ⊆ker F does not appear in the rule.
  The refinement relation is one of inclusion: a suﬀicient encoder retains at least the dis-
tinctions the declared tasks need and may retain more. Equality of the two relations would

Chapter 17

Correspondence




The preceding parts concern what a verified result is and how it is produced, inherited
and repaired. This part concerns the step that turns a verified theorem into a statement
about the world, the step that Chapter 9 placed at layers O2 and O3 and that no kernel can
check. The chapter does three things.  It states what a correspondence claim consists of
and proves that a claim with no preregistered failure condition is compatible with every
observation (Section 17.1). It treats the question of whether parameters can be recovered
from observations as a suﬀiciency question and proves the local and global versions of the
answer to be genuinely different (Sections 17.2 and 17.3). And it works one complete ex-
ample, the Burgers equation, in which a verifiable theorem has an explicit scope boundary
that coincides exactly with the failure of a local-to-global argument (Section 17.4).


17.1  Correspondence claims and failure conditions

Definition 17.1 (Correspondence claim). A correspondence claim is a tuple C = (φ, ι, τ, Obs, Fail)
where

   • φ is a formal statement with a checked proof (layer O1 discharged);
   • ι is an interpretation that assigns to the formal symbols of φ quantities of a described
     system (layer O2);
   • τ is an operationalization: a procedure that turns a record of measurements into values
      of the quantities assigned by ι (layer O3);
   • Obs is the set of possible observation records; and
   • Fail ⊆Obs is the failure condition, a decidable set fixed before observation.
The claim survives a record r ∈Obs if r /∈Fail and fails on r otherwise.

Proposition 17.2 (Failure conditions carry the empirical content).  (a)  If Fail =  ∅, the
      claim survives every record.
 (b) Let C and C′ differ only in the failure condition, with Fail′ ⊊Fail. Then every record on which
      C′ fails is a record on which C fails, and any r ∈Fail\Fail′ is a record on which C fails and C′
      survives. In particular a failure condition modified after r was seen can convert failure into
      survival, and the two claims are different claims although the formal theorem φ is the same.
  (c) The survival relation is a function of the pair (Fail, r); it is not a function of r alone, nor of φ
      alone.

Proof. (a) r /∈∅. (b) is immediate from Fail′ ⊆Fail. (c) Survival is r /∈Fail. Distinct

failure conditions give distinct survival functions, and φ does not appear in the definition
of survival.                                           ■

theorem together with an interpretation and an operationalization defines what is claimed
only up to the failure condition; changing the latter after the fact changes the claim. This

17.2  Identifiability is suﬀiciency of the observation


A frequent correspondence claim is that parameters θ of a model can be recovered from
observations y = F(θ). In the vocabulary of Chapter 10, let H be the parameter space,
F  : H →Y the observation map as a representation, and rec : H →H the identity, the
task of recovering the parameter.

Proposition 17.3 (Identifiability). The task rec is F-computable if and only if F is injective. For
a weaker task T  : H →Z (a function of the parameter, such as one coordinate or a derived quantity),
T is recoverable from F if and only if T is constant on the fibres of F.


Proof. Proposition 1.12 applied to the representation F. The first statement is the case T =
id, for which constancy on fibres means that each fibre is a singleton.           ■


  Thus a proof that “the observations determine the parameters” is a proof of injectiv-
ity, and a proof that a particular quantity is determined is a proof of constancy on fibres.
The diﬀiculty in practice is that injectivity is a global property while the tools that prove it
cheaply are local.


17.3  Local versus global injectivity

Let F  : Rn →Rn be C1.

Chapter 18

Mutation of Verified Artifacts




Chapters 11 and 12 derived, from the structure of a checker, predictions about which de-
pendents of a verified development survive a change. A prediction is a claim, and the way
to test it is to change the development and see. This chapter formalizes that experiment:
what a mutation is, what a preregistered prediction is, how predictions are scored and re-
tained, and why a model that sees a dependency graph without edge types is not merely
less accurate but insuﬀicient for the task. It also treats the two audit rules that protect the ex-
periment from a failure specific to proof assistants, namely that an artifact can be accepted
while resting on a placeholder.

  The experimental work that motivated this chapter, a frozen Lean 4 development, a
preregistered matrix of twenty mutants over twelve operator classes, and a batch run over
all of them, is described in the author’s separate manuscripts [39]. Per-mutant outcome
tables are not reproduced here. What is established in this chapter is the mathematics of
the experimental design and what the design can and cannot support.


18.1  Specimens, operators, outcomes


Definition 18.1 (Specimen, mutation, blast set). A specimen is a well-formed environment
Γ in the sense of Section 12.4, together with a set Ax0 of declared axioms. A mutation operator
is a partial function µ taking a specimen and a target constant to a new environment Γ′ =
µ(Γ, c). The blast set of the mutant is

               B(Γ, Γ′) = {e a constant of Γ′ : e does not check in Γ′},

where “checks” is as in Lemma 12.15. The footprint change is ∆Ax(e) = AxΓ′(e) △AxΓ(e)
for each constant e that checks in both.

  An operator class groups operators by the kind of change: replacing a theorem body
by another proof of the same type, replacing a definition body, changing a declared type,
renaming, reordering, normalizing associativity, and so on.

Definition 18.2 (Prediction, correctness, soundness, precision). A predictor is a function bB
from (specimen, operator, target) to a set of constants. On a mutant it is sound if B ⊆bB,
precise if bB ⊆B, and correct if both. A prediction concerning footprint is a prediction of
∆Ax for each surviving constant.

                                      108

18.2. PREREGISTRATION AND RETENTION                                   109


  Soundness and precision are independent: a predictor that always returns every con-
stant is sound and imprecise, and one that always returns the empty set is precise when-
ever B = ∅and unsound otherwise. The experimental question is whether a model yields
predictions that are both.


18.2  Preregistration and retention


Definition 18.3 (Prediction log). A prediction log is an append-only sequence of entries
(id, model, pred, timep, out, timeo), where pred is a prediction made under the model model
at time timep, and out is an observed outcome recorded at timeo. An entry is preregistered if
timep < timemut, the time at which the mutant artifact first existed. An entry is falsified under
its model if pred̸ = out (for the exact notion), and retained if it remains in the log unchanged.
A model amendment adds a new model identifier; it never modifies existing entries.

Proposition 18.4 (Retention prevents retroactive correction). In a prediction log satisfying
the append-only rule:

  (a) the set of entries falsified under their models is nondecreasing in time;
  (b) for each mutant, the score of a model amended after timeo on that mutant is a retrodiction,
      not a prediction: its timep is later than timeo, so the entry is not preregistered;
  (c) the proportion of preregistered predictions that were correct under model m is defined only for
     mutants whose entries for m precede the mutant artifact, and is therefore not affected by later
     amendments.

Proof. (a) Entries are never modified or deleted, and falsification is a property of a sin-
gle entry. (b) The amended model has timep > timeo ≥timemut. (c) is the definition of
preregistration restricted to a model.                             ■

  The proposition states, in the form of an invariant, the practice of preserving a miss as
a miss. An amended model may correctly describe the mutants that falsified its predeces-
sor; that correct description is evidence of fit and not of predictive ability. Evidence of
predictive ability for the amended model requires new preregistered mutants.

manuscripts cited above, is that a dependency representation that merges the relations of

and it is provable.

18.6  What a matrix of this size can support


A preregistered matrix of n mutants partitions its operator classes into at most n cells. A
predictor that agrees with the observed outcomes on all n mutants is indistinguishable,
by this matrix, from every other predictor with the same values on those mutants, and

112                     CHAPTER 18. MUTATION OF VERIFIED ARTIFACTS


a class represented by a single mutant is represented by a single point: agreement on it
cannot separate a model that is right for the class from one that is right for the instance. In
the language of Chapter 10, the matrix is a task family, and its closure is exactly the set of
functions of the n outcomes. Claims about a class that go beyond the mutants of that class
are not supported by the matrix, whatever its size elsewhere. No numerical statistic over
the twenty mutants is computed in this book.


18.7  What this chapter fixes


  (1) A mutation experiment is a function from mutants to blast sets, and a prediction
  is sound, precise or correct (Definition 18.2). (2) Retention of falsified predictions is
  an invariant of an append-only log, and a model amended after the fact is evaluated
  by retrodiction (Proposition 18.4). (3) The flat dependency graph does not determine
  the outcome of body replacements, so no flat predictor is correct; typed edges give a
  sound predictor (Propositions 18.6 and 18.7). (4) Placeholder audits read footprints
  on the final environment and treat footprint change as a distinct outcome (Proposi-
  tion 18.10). (5) Semantic preservation of a statement does not carry the proof term
  (Proposition 18.11).

Chapter 19

A Negative Result as Method




The preceding chapters describe what a verified result owes the reader. This chapter de-
scribes what a negative result owes, using as its worked case a reported simulation study
in which a proposed decomposition of a physical phenomenon was tested and did not
earn its place [40]. The study concerns the onset of motility-induced phase separation
and tests whether features named capacity and dissipation add predictive information be-
yond density. The findings reported there, which are simulation findings and not physical
laboratory replication, are three: the simulation engine was validated; the decomposition
supplied no incremental predictive value beyond density that survived replication; and an
intervention pilot was underpowered, leaving causal content unresolved. Numbers from
that study are not reproduced here. The chapter proves what each of the three statements
does and does not license, in a form independent of the particular system.


19.1  Two questions that must not be merged


Let θ range over parameters of a simulated system and let E(θ) be an outcome produced
by the engine. Let b(θ) be a baseline feature (here, density) and ϕ(θ) a proposed additional
feature.

Definition 19.1 (Engine validation and decomposition evaluation). Engine validation is the
claim that E computes the intended model: on a benchmark set B of problems with inde-
pendently known answers, E agrees with them to a declared tolerance. This is a claim of
the layers O1 and O2 of Chapter 9 for the engine. Decomposition evaluation is the claim that
the features (b, ϕ) stand in a declared relation to the outcome, here that ϕ adds predictive
information about E beyond b.

Proposition 19.2 (The two are independent). Engine validation neither implies nor is implied
by a positive decomposition claim. In particular a validated engine can yield a decomposition that
adds nothing, and an engine failing validation can yield a decomposition that appears to add predic-
tive value.

Proof. Validation concerns the map θ 7→E(θ) against B. The decomposition claim concerns
the joint law of (E(θ), b(θ), ϕ(θ)) under a sampling distribution of θ. Take an engine that
computes E(θ) = g(b(θ)) exactly:  it is validated by construction against any benchmark
that g solves, and ϕ adds nothing under every distribution. Take an engine with a bug that

adds predictive value.                                     ■

  The separation is not a courtesy. A negative decomposition result is informative only if
the engine is trusted, and a positive one is informative only if the same holds; but neither
follows from the other, and a report that merges them cannot be read.

Chapter 20

What a Verified Result Owes




The book began from a pair of questions: what does a verification assure, and what must a
verified result keep in order to remain useful? The chapters between give answers in pieces,
each proved where it is stated. This chapter collects them as three principles, converts them
into a list of items that a verified result should carry, and states plainly which parts of the
book are proved, which are cited, which were checked by computation, and which are
proposals.



20.1  Three principles


  Principle 1: Assurance attaches to the checker and the bridge, never to the producer,
  and failure to certify is not certification of failure.
 A proof system is a producer together with a decidable checking relation (Defini-
  tion 1.1); soundness of the producer is irrelevant to the assurance (Theorem 1.5); the
  assurance of a translated result is the conjunction of the checker’s and the translation’s
  (Proposition 1.7); a verified statement is bridged to an observation through layers O1
  to O3 of which a kernel can discharge only the first (Chapter 9). A report of preserva-
  tion has three values, and the third is not a failure (Theorem 12.6). A gate that sees only
  what the proposer sees cannot discriminate what the proposer cannot (Theorem 15.8).



  Principle 2: Suﬀiciency is always suﬀiciency for a declared task, and the declaration
  is part of the result.
 A representation serves a task exactly when the task is constant on its fibres (Propo-
  sition 1.12, Theorem 10.4); a declared family has a minimal artifact and a closure of
  served tasks (Theorem 10.7); every non-injective representation fails some task (Theo-
  rem 10.12). A certificate is a region and a verdict is a point (Theorems 11.2 and 11.10);
  repair is a relation, and local repair is impossible from a representation that identifies
  distant artifacts (Theorems 11.13 and 11.15).



  Principle 3: A collapse is admissible only relative to a declared task and the refusals
  on record.

  In a search, the option space is changed only by refusal and collapse (Proposition 13.5);
  a refusal is lossless iff the refused item is redundant for the declared option closure
  (Theorem 14.4); fair runs with admissible deletion remain complete (Theorem 14.7);

  The principles are consequences of a single observation, that a function factors through
a quotient if and only if it respects the equivalence the quotient imposes. Their content is
what follows when the observation is applied to the objects of automated reasoning: runs,
certificates, worlds, dependency graphs, observation records.

20.4  Open directions


Mechanization.  The lifecycle machine, the interface lemma and the stability results of
Chapter 11 are small enough to be formalized. A formalization of the lifecycle in a proof
assistant would also be a test of the claims of Chapter 18: the typed predictor makes a
prediction about the effect of mutating that very development.

122                       CHAPTER 20. WHAT A VERIFIED RESULT OWES


Beyond propositional deletion.  Theorem 14.7 uses finiteness of the clause universe. For
first-order resolution the persistence argument needs a well-founded ordering on clauses
and redundancy defined relative to smaller clauses, as in the model-based completeness
theorems of Bachmair and Ganzinger [2]. Combining that machinery with the world
model, with refusal records as first-class objects, is a task of the same kind as Chapter 14
at greater technical cost.


Scoped certificates and gluing. A certificate with its scope can be regarded as a local ob-
ject over the regime in which it was verified, with restriction to a smaller regime (a narrower
scope, a subset of the assumptions) and compatibility conditions on overlaps (agreement
on shared variables and assumptions). Whether the resulting structure supports a useful
gluing theorem, and whether an obstruction to gluing is detected by cohomological invari-
ants, depends on a particular choice of base space and coeﬀicients, which has not been
constructed in this book. The proposal is recorded here as a programmatic remark and is
not a result.


Certified fragments of practical interest.  Example 12.9 gives a complete fragment for
propositional rewriting. The corresponding fragments for linear arithmetic, bit-vectors
and rewriting modulo theories, with certificates in the sense of Definition 12.5, are the
natural next cases.


Exact prediction.  Proposition 18.6 gives a sound predictor of the blast set and no more.
Exact prediction for definitional unfolding requires deciding convertibility of replacement
bodies, which is checker-dependent.


20.5  Conclusion


A verification is a function from a statement and a derivation to a verdict. Everything that
makes the verdict useful, that it be about the right statement, that it survive what changes,
that it be repairable, auditable and extendable, is information that the function does not
return and that the run, the dependency graph and the surrounding record contain or
lose. The preceding chapters show that this information has precise structure: partitions
and their refinements, regions and their margins, options and their refusals, versions and
their obligations. A result that carries it can be reused; one that does not can be rechecked
and nothing more. The contribution of the book is to say exactly which information, for
which task, and what it costs to keep.

External Theorems Used




The following results are used in the text and are stated here as they are used. They are
cited, not proved. Entries are in the order of first use. Where the text proves a special case
(Newman’s lemma, propositional resolution completeness, the Nelson–Oppen counterex-
ample), the proof is in the chapter indicated.

A.1 Church and Turing (Chapter 2, 12).
  The set of valid first-order sentences over a signature containing a binary relation symbol
    is recursively enumerable and not decidable [7, 34].

A.2 Compactness (Chapter 3).
  A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if each finite subset does (Gödel;
   Mal’cev).

A.3 Herbrand’s theorem (Chapter 3).
  A set of universal clauses is unsatisfiable if and only if some finite set of its ground
   instances is propositionally unsatisfiable [15].

A.4 Lifting lemma (Chapter 3).
    If clauses C′, D′ are ground instances of C, D by a common substitution and E′ is a
   resolvent of C′, D′, then C, D have a resolvent E (using a most general unifier) of which
   E′ is an instance [27].

A.5 Birkhoff’s completeness theorem (Chapter 4).
  An equation s ≈t holds in all models of an equational theory E if and only if it is
   derivable from E by the rules of equational logic [4].

A.6 Knuth–Bendix completion (Chapter 4).
  Given a finite set of equations and a reduction order, a fair run of the completion pro-
   cedure that does not fail on an unorientable equation produces a convergent rewrite
  system generating the same equational theory [17, 16, 3].

A.7 Tseitin transformation (Chapter 12).
  Every propositional formula has an equisatisfiable clause form of size linear in the for-
   mula, over extra variables [33].

A.8 Cook–Reckhow (Chapter 8).
  There exists a propositional proof system in which every tautology has a proof of poly-
  nomial size if and only if NP = coNP [9].
